Abstract:
<jats:p>Wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) offers high deposition efficiency for large-scale aluminum components; however, layer-by-layer thermal cycling often induces microstructural anisotropy and spatial heterogeneity, which compromise structural reliability. In this study, an ultrasonic-based quantitative framework is proposed to evaluate and optimize anisotropy and heterogeneity in WAAM 2319 aluminum alloy. Nine blocks were fabricated using an orthogonal design with three key process parameters: torch travel speed, arc current, and shielding gas flow rate. Ultrasonic velocity and attenuation were employed to construct anisotropy and heterogeneity indicators. Results show that velocity-based anisotropy remains below 0.53%, indicating nearly isotropic elastic stiffness, whereas attenuation-based anisotropy reaches up to 76%, revealing pronounced direction-dependent microstructural and porosity features. Metallographic analysis confirms that grain morphology variation and interlayer porosity jointly govern attenuation responses. Response surface surrogate models were established to correlate ultrasonic indicators with process parameters, and both single- and multi-objective optimizations were performed within the feasible process window. The proposed framework provides a non-destructive, volumetric approach for microstructure-informed process parameter optimization in WAAM aluminum alloys.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing systems frequently fail to predict process instability before thermal disturbances generate porosity, cracking, spatter, lack of fusion, distortion, and inconsistent layer consolidation, partly because sensor data, machine settings, thermal models, and quality evidence remain fragmented. This study aimed to develop and quantitatively evaluate an integrated thermal behavior modeling framework for improving Process-Instability Prediction Effectiveness across operational additive manufacturing cases. A quantitative, cross-sectional, descriptive, explanatory, and case-based design was applied to industrial manufacturing facilities, research centers, university laboratories, technology providers, and quality-testing organizations using laser powder-bed fusion, directed-energy deposition, electron-beam melting, and related metal additive manufacturing systems. From 350 distributed questionnaires, 312 valid responses were retained, yielding an effective response rate of 89.14 percent. The model examined Thermal-Process Data Quality and Integration, Heat-Input Consistency and Energy Control, Thermal-Gradient and Heat-Accumulation Management, Melt-Pool Thermal Stability, Cooling and Solidification Behavior Control, Real-Time Thermal Monitoring and Modeling Capability, and Process-Instability Prediction Effectiveness. Five-point Likert data were analyzed in SPSS using descriptive statistics, reliability and validity tests, Pearson correlations, ANOVA, assumption diagnostics, and multiple regression. Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from .831 to .914, KMO reached .902, and Bartlett’s test was significant, χ² (595) = 4,582.63, p < .001. Process-Instability Prediction Effectiveness recorded M = 4.07, SD = .57. All six predictors were significant, and the model explained 68.9 percent of outcome variance, R² = .689, adjusted R² = .683, F (6, 305) = 112.61, p < .001. Melt-Pool Thermal Stability was strongest, β = .26, followed by data quality, β = .23, and real-time monitoring, β = .21. The findings imply that coordinated thermal data, energy control, melt-pool stabilization, cooling management, and real-time modeling can strengthen early warnings, reduce defect-generating variation, improve process control, and support more reliable additive manufacturing quality decisions. They provide evidence to prioritize monitoring investments, calibration, model validation, and workforce training.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This article considers the use of additive manufacturing to produce cutting tools for various machining operations, especially turning, milling, and drilling. The right geometry and material of the tool as well as coatings applied on cutting edges are crucial as they improve the life and performance of the tool. The study described here focused on a four-flute end mill made of maraging steel 1.2709 using a Concept Laser M2 Cusing Direct Metal Laser Melting (DMLM) machine. Before the printed tool was first used, it was examined to determine its dimensional and geometric accuracy, surface roughness, and surface structure. The measurement data showed that the tool required machining, e.g., grinding, to improve its geometry because the total runout of the shank and the cutting edge radius were too high, amounting to 120 μm and 217 μm, respectively. The cutting edges were sharpened to obtain a fully functional cutting tool ready to perform milling operations. The study aimed to check the dimensional and geometric accuracy of the 3D printed milling cutter and determine the optimal machining allowance for its finishing.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) processes are flexible and efficient technologies for producing complex geometries. However, ensuring reliability and repeatability is challenging due to the complex physics and various sources of uncertainty in the process. In this work, we investigate closed-loop control of the melt pool dimensions in a 2-D laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process. We propose a trajectory optimization-based layer-to-layer (L2L) controller based on a linear parameter-varying (LPV) model that adjusts the laser power input to the next layer to track a desired melt pool depth and validate our controller by placing it in closed-loop high-fidelity multilayer smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulator of the 2-D LPBF process. Detailed numerical case studies demonstrate successful regulation of the melt pool depth on brick and overhang geometries and provide first of its kind results on the effectiveness of L2L input optimization for the LPBF process as well as detailed insight into the physics of the controlled process. Computational complexity and process performance results illustrate the method’s effectiveness and provide an outlook for its implementation onto real systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Powder-bed arc additive manufacturing (PBAAM) may reduce the cost of powder-bed metal additive manufacturing and enable thicker layers than laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), but melt-track stability limits are not well established. Here, 316L stainless steel powder (15–53 µm) was melted by a TIG-based arc in a custom powder-bed system while varying current, travel speed, layer thickness and hatch distance. Single tracks on an inclined bed (≈0–0.4 mm thickness) were used to identify continuity loss and melt-pool width, quantified from top-view images via width profiles, a gap-based continuity metric and the coefficient of variation. Parallel-track tests at 0.15, 0.20 and 0.25 mm layer thickness with hatch distances set to 25%, 50% and 75% of the measured melt-pool width assessed inter-track bonding and lack of fusion, and selected parameters were validated in five-layer builds. Higher current with low-to-moderate travel speeds produced wider, more stable melt pools on the inclined bed. Hatch ratios of 25–50% were the most effective for sustaining fusion in single layers and multi-layer builds, whereas 75% promoted unbonded regions and narrow-track morphologies. Overall, PBAAM can process substantially thicker layers with relatively simple equipment, but requires a narrow, carefully tuned window to balance continuity, fusion and heat accumulation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing is an emerging 3D printing technique for the fabrication of advanced metal components. Widespread adoption of it and similar additive technologies is hampered by poor understanding of laser-metal interactions under such extreme thermal regimes. Here, we elucidate the mechanism of pore formation and liquid-solid interface dynamics during typical laser powder bed fusion conditions using in situ X-ray imaging and multi-physics simulations. Pores are revealed to form during changes in laser scan velocity due to the rapid formation then collapse of deep keyhole depressions in the surface which traps inert shielding gas in the solidifying metal. We develop a universal mitigation strategy which eliminates this pore formation process and improves the geometric quality of melt tracks. Our results provide insight into the physics of laser-metal interaction and demonstrate the potential for science-based approaches to improve confidence in components produced by laser powder bed fusion. Laser-matter interactions during laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing remain poorly understood. Here, the authors combine in situ X-ray imaging and finite element simulations to show how detrimental pores form under printing conditions and develop a strategy to suppress them.

Khairallah et al. used experiments and a multiphysics model to determine the origin of the melt spatter and defect formation that degrade the properties of built parts (see the Perspective by Polonsky and Pollock). Science, this issue p. 660; see also p. 583 Multiscale physics models help isolate a stability criterion that is useful for avoiding defects in laser bed powder fusion printing. State-of-the-art metal 3D printers promise to revolutionize manufacturing, yet they have not reached optimal operational reliability. The challenge is to control complex laser–powder–melt pool interdependency (dependent upon each other) dynamics. We used high-fidelity simulations, coupled with synchrotron experiments, to capture fast multitransient dynamics at the meso-nanosecond scale and discovered new spatter-induced defect formation mechanisms that depend on the scan strategy and a competition between laser shadowing and expulsion. We derived criteria to stabilize the melt pool dynamics and minimize defects. This will help improve build reliability.

Abstract:
Grinding tools with superabrasive grains can be manufactured from different bond materials. In several industrial applications, metallic bond systems are used. In general, these show good grain retention and offer a high thermal conductivity, when compared to the other widely used bond types such as vitrified and resin bonds. One drawback of the metallic bond is the lack of pores in the grinding layer. This is caused by the manufacturing processes that are typically used, like brazing or hot pressing. These generally produce very dense layers. The high density and low porosity lead to comparatively little space for the transport of lubricant, coolant, and chips. One approach to eliminate this disadvantage is to introduce cavities into the grinding layer, using the laser powder bed fusion technique (LPBF). In order to evaluate the general suitability of LPBF in combination with the bond material and diamond grains, grinding layer samples with a nickel-titanium bond were produced. The abrasive behavior of these samples was tested in scratch tests on cemented carbide to verify the applicability as grinding tools. While the diamond grains in the powder mixture are not part of the fusion process, they also did not interfere with the manufacturing process, and the scratch tests showed promising abrasive capabilities. The grinding layer itself withstood the process forces, and no grain breakout could be observed. This indicates that the grain retention forces are high enough for the grinding process and that NiTi has a high potential as a bonding material for the manufacturing of grinding tools via LPBF.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigates the effects of Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) treatment on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF)-manufactured Hastelloy H. This research evaluates the trade-offs between defect elimination, anisotropy reduction, and strength retention in well-optimized LPBF components. Specimens were manufactured using optimized LPBF parameters, achieving 99.85% density, and then subjected to HIP treatment at 1160 °C/100 MPa for 4 h. The analysis includes porosity analysis, grain size measurement, crystallographic texture evaluation, and tensile tests in two principal orientations. The results show that HIP treatment provides minimal benefits for defect elimination in already high-quality LPBF material, reducing porosity from 0.15% to <0.01%—a negligible improvement that does not translate to proportional mechanical enhancement. Tensile tests show that as-built specimens exhibited orientation-dependent strength, with XY-oriented samples reaching a yield strength (YS) of 682 MPa, ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 864 MPa, and elongation of 17%, while XZ-oriented samples showed lower strength (YS = 621 MPa, UTS = 653 MPa) but superior ductility (elongation = 47%). After HIP treatment, anisotropy was largely removed, with both XY and XZ orientations showing comparable strength (YS ≈ 315–317 MPa, UTS ≈ 682–691 MPa) and elongation (38–41%). This indicates that HIP significantly improves ductility and isotropy at the cost of reduced strength. HIP treatment effectively eliminates the anisotropy of LPBF components, achieving uniform hardness across all orientations while reducing crystallographic texture intensity from 12.3× to 3.2× random orientation. This isotropy improvement occurs through grain-coarsening mechanisms that increase the average grain size from 7.5 μm to 13.5 μm, eliminating cellular–dendritic strengthening structures and reducing hardness by 32% (254 HV2 to 170 HV2) following Hall–Petch relationships. The conducted research confirms that HIP treatment allows for modification of the microstructure of Hastelloy X alloy, which may lead to the improvement of its mechanical properties in high-temperature applications and a significant increase in the isotropy of the material.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The considerable expense associated with metal additive manufacturing (AM), partly attributed to the high costs of raw materials, forms a significant obstacle hindering the widespread adoption and scaling of this technology. In response to this challenge, this study endeavors to explore and optimize the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process parameters for Ti-6Al-4V powders with offsize (45–106 µm) and wide (15–106 µm) particle size distribution (PSD) which are more cost-effective. The outcomes will be compared to those of the same alloy with a standard 15–53 µm PSD. The primary focus of this investigation revolves around two key objectives: firstly, establishing correlations between the laser powder bed fusion process parameters and the resulting density, hardness, and roughness. This objective is achieved by investigating the impact of process parameters within the context of the contour–skin–core method. Secondly, the porosity, microstructure, elemental composition, and dimensional fidelity of several components made from the offsize and wide powders were investigated, utilizing the optimized process parameters for density. To this end, an efficient multi-step experimental design and optimization process was adopted. The findings resulted in the identification of correlations between the significant process parameters and the studied responses, enabling the achievement of 98.7% density and 40.6 HRC hardness for offsize powder and 98.7% density and 40 HRC hardness for wide powder. A separate set of optimized process parameters for larger geometries produced densities exceeding 99.9% in both as-built and HIP conditions across all three powders. Additionally, the results confirmed the higher sensitivity of the roughness to powder size, with the optimized values fluctuating between 9.5 µm and 15.7 µm. Comprehensive microstructural investigation reveals no significant differences in phase evolution or grain structure resulting from the use of offsize or wide powders. This study confirms the viability of utilizing powders containing a higher portion of large particles to mitigate the costs associated with LPBF processes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In metallurgy, mechanical deformation is essential to engineer the microstructure of metals and to tailor their mechanical properties. However, this practice is inapplicable to near-net-shape metal parts produced by additive manufacturing (AM), since it would irremediably compromise their carefully designed geometries. In this work, we show how to circumvent this limitation by controlling the dislocation density and thermal stability of a steel alloy produced by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology. We show that by manipulating the alloy’s solidification structure, we can ‘program’ recrystallization upon heat treatment without using mechanical deformation. When employed site-specifically, our strategy enables designing and creating complex microstructure architectures that combine recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions with different microstructural features and properties. We show how this heterogeneity may be conducive to materials with superior performance compared to those with monolithic microstructure. Our work inspires the design of high-performance metal parts with artificially engineered microstructures by AM.

This study investigates the application of topology optimization (TO) in combination with laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) to design a lightweight, high-performance bicycle pedal crank using AlSi10Mg alloy. The optimization process was carried out using Fusion 360 and nTopology, resulting in a 20% mass reduction while ensuring compliance with the ISO 14781 standards for pedal cranks. The microstructure exhibited the characteristic melt pool patterns associated with LPBF, indicative of the manufacturing process. Surface roughness measurements showed a mean value of 23.4 μm, with dimensional analysis revealing a mean deviation of 7% from nominal dimensions. The powder distribution analysis indicated a narrow particle size distribution, contributing to consistent print quality. The component’s hardness was measured at 134 HV0.3, highlighting its promising mechanical properties. This work demonstrates the potential of TO and LPBF to produce structurally optimized, lightweight components with enhanced performance, providing valuable insights into the application of Design for Additive Manufacturing for metallic materials.

Post-processing and trial-and-error adjustment of processing conditions to reduce porosity are time-consuming and expensive. Here, we combined mechanistic modeling and experimental data analysis and proposed an easy-to-use, verifiable, dimensionless gas porosity index to mitigate pore formation. The results from the mechanistic model were rigorously tested against independent experimental data. Based on the results, a gas porosity map was constructed that can be used in practice for selecting appropriate sets of process variables to mitigate gas porosity without the need for empirical testing. Computational modeling of Ti-6Al-4V additive manufacturing (AM) represents a transformative paradigm for aerospace and medical engineering; however, industrial adoption remains hindered by a persistent conundrum in structural integrity and process reliability. This gap-oriented review provides a critical synthesis of 117 computational studies published between 2014 and 2026, analyzing the convergence of thermomechanical finite element analysis, mesoscopic microstructure models, and AI-enhanced optimization. By evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of many methodologies, we identify three fundamental barriers to industrial certification: (i) a ten-order-of-magnitude scale disconnect between micro-fidelity and part-scale tractability; (ii) a physics crisis arising from the systematic neglect of solid-state phase transformation strains, leading to residual stress errors exceeding 500% and distortion overpredictions of 461%; and (iii) the defect–microstructure paradox, where stochastic porosity reduces fatigue strength by up to 85% yet remains isolated from deterministic grain models. The paper examines the challenges of model interoperability and uncertainty propagation across the process-structure-property chain. Ultimately, this review aims to guide future research by providing insights into the potential of integrated, uncertainty-aware digital twins to achieve predictive convergence within the 95% confidence intervals necessary for safety-critical applications.

Abstract:
The need to optimize the processing conditions of additively manufactured (AM) metals and alloys has driven advances in throughput capabilities for material property measurements such as tensile strength or hardness. High-throughput (HT) characterization of AM metal microstructure has fallen significantly behind the pace of property measurements due to intrinsic bottlenecks associated with the artisan and labor-intensive preparation methods required to produce highly polished surfaces. This inequality in data throughput has led to a reliance on heuristics to connect process to structure or structure to properties for AM structural materials. In this study, we show a transformative approach to achieve laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) printing, HT preparation using dry electropolishing and HT electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). This approach was used to construct a library of > 600 experimental EBSD sample sets spanning a diverse range of LPBF process conditions for AM Kovar. This vast library is far more expansive in parameter space than most state-of-the-art studies, yet it required only approximately 10 labor hours to acquire. Build geometries, surface preparation methods, and microscopy details, as well as the entire library of >600 EBSD data sets over the two sample design versions, have been shared with intent for the materials community to leverage the data and further advance the approach. Using this library, we investigated process–structure relationships and uncovered an unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build, when varied, using otherwise identical laser parameters.

Abstract:
With the increasing adoption of metal additive manufacturing (AM), researchers and practitioners are turning to data-driven approaches to optimise printing conditions. Cross-sectional images of melt tracks provide valuable information for tuning process parameters, developing parameter scaling data, and identifying defects. Here we present an image segmentation neural network that automatically identifies and measures melt track dimensions from a cross-section image. We use a U-Net architecture to train on a data set of 62 pre-labelled images obtained from different labs, machines, and materials coupled with image augmentation. When neural network hyperparameters such as batch size and learning rate are properly tuned, the learned model shows an accuracy for classification of over 99% and an F1 score over 90%. The neural network exhibits robustness when tested on images captured by various users, printed on different machines, and acquired using different microscopes. A post-processing module extracts the height and width of the melt pool, and the wetting angles. We discuss opportunities to improve model performance and avenues for transfer learning, such as extension to other AM processes such as directed energy deposition.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing (AM) requires process-comparison tools that remain practical when sample generation and testing are costly. We propose a univariate, nonparametric workflow for comparing a candidate AM process to a stable reference process by testing distributional equivalency for a single response variable. The method discretizes the reference distribution into empirical percentile-defined bins and combines this representation with a sequential sampling protocol designed to reduce unnecessary sampling when evidence for equivalency or non-equivalency becomes sufficient. Simulation studies were used to evaluate operating characteristics across experimental settings, and a validation case study based on geometric measurements of laser based powder bed fusion plate scans correctly classified a candidate process expected to be equivalent to the reference while identifying a non-equivalent process at the first sampling step. The workflow is most appropriate for low-sample, high-cost, or throughput-constrained settings, and is best viewed as a tool for process comparability, change control, calibration, and requalification support rather than as a standalone replacement for qualification standards. The full workflow is implemented in the open-source AMEquivalency package to support reproducible analysis.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Additive manufacturing has emerged as a key enabling technology for in-space manufacturing, offering the potential to reduce logistics mass, enhance mission autonomy, and support long-duration exploration. The suppression of gravity-driven phenomena fundamentally alters melt pool dynamics, heat transfer, surface-tension-dominated flow, and defect formation, limiting the direct transferability of terrestrial AM process knowledge to space applications. This paper reviews the current understanding of metallic additive manufacturing process physics under reduced gravity, with emphasis on melt pool behavior, dimensional stability, and in situ monitoring constraints. Approaches for qualification and certification are critically examined, including the applicability of existing AM standards, the role of digital twins and model-based verification, and emerging strategies for space-based validation. Enabling technologies such as autonomous and AI-assisted fabrication, compact hardware architectures, and alternative energy sources are discussed in the context of reliable in-space operation. By synthesizing current developments and identifying key limitations and open challenges, the review provides a roadmap for advancing additive manufacturing toward operational readiness, supporting sustainable exploration, in-space infrastructure development, and long-duration human presence beyond low Earth orbit.</jats:p>

The demonstrated design used small 4 mm × 3 mm columns representing combinations of five laser powers, four scan speeds, and three material conditions in LPBF IN625. Small column dimensions limit laser travel compared with regular samples, altering thermal histories, cooling rates, temperature gradients, and potentially microstructure and hardness. Therefore, miniature combinatorial specimens should not automatically be assumed to reproduce bulk-cube density or porosity results. Neighboring-column thermal effects were investigated using repeated process conditions; measured microstructure and hardness suggested these effects were minimal, partly because lack-of-fusion porosity between columns provided thermal isolation. The authors suggest thicker porous dividers or gaps of unmelted powder to further reduce heat transfer, with thermal modeling useful for optimization. The approach substantially reduces material, preparation, processing, and setup effort, estimated at approximately five times faster than producing individual regular samples. However, the authors explicitly caution that combinatorial-sample information is not equivalent to regular-sample information, so validation against bulk specimens is necessary when screening density or porosity.

The excerpt does not directly study thin-wall orientation relative to the recoater blade or gas-flow direction, nor does it quantify wall swelling, deflection, local powder-layer thickness, or melt-pool geometry. It does, however, identify mechanisms relevant to those questions. Shielding gas typically flows from right to left, and spatter and condensate can be transported and deposited preferentially along this path. Gas velocity decreases downstream, changing the ability of the flow to carry particles; deposited particles may become embedded in consolidating regions and act as failure-initiation sites. Consequently, mechanical properties and porosity-related quality can vary with position on the powder bed. The text also indicates that inconsistent gas flow, dosing/wiper action, and thermal history produce spatial variation, while uniform energy distribution and controlled thermal conditions improve repeatability. For thin walls, distortion or peeling that raises a wall above the nominal bed can interfere with the recoater, alter the wiper-to-build-plane gap, and produce inconsistent powder layers or a failed build. Hard and soft recoaters also behave differently: hard wipers tolerate greater deformation, whereas soft wipers exert less load on delicate structures. These points support considering wall orientation, upstream/downstream placement, and proximity to gas-flow or recoater paths, but the excerpt provides no direct orientation-specific experimental results.

The excerpt provides relevant evidence for how spatter, inert-gas flow, and recoating can influence LPBF porosity and surface damage, but it does not directly compare thin-wall orientations relative to the recoater blade or gas-flow direction, nor does it discuss wall deflection/swelling, local powder-layer thickness variation, or build-plate position effects on melt-pool behavior. Spatter may be generated or transported by inert-gas flow and can deposit either on the powder bed ahead of future scan vectors or on previously solidified tracks before recoating. Because spatter particles are often much larger than the feedstock and have altered surface properties, they require more energy to remelt and can produce lack-of-fusion (LoF) porosity. Large spatter particles are particularly consequential; for IN-718, particles above approximately 770 micrometres equivalent spherical diameter had a reported 100% probability of causing an LoF pore. During recoating, strongly adhered particles can damage the blade, while loose particles may be swept across the bed and create deep troughs, affecting subsequent layers. The excerpt also identifies conduction and stable-keyhole processing as regimes that reduce spatter formation. Thus, it supports investigation of orientation-dependent spatter deposition and recoater interactions, but provides no direct positional or directional experimental conclusions.

It states that spatter becomes suspended in the gas flow and that gas flowing across the powder bed carries particulate matter toward filtration and recirculation systems. Gas temperature affects particulate-carrying capacity: cooler gas improves pickup, while uncontrolled heating can produce a dirty chamber and may lead to particles depositing on optical windows. These observations could help contextualize spatter deposition near thin walls, although no wall-specific deposition measurements are reported. The excerpt also identifies process parameters, part geometry, scan strategies, and ambient conditions as factors affecting LPBF density. It emphasizes that scan strategies define scan paths and melt-pool boundaries, thereby influencing density, surface finish, and pore formation. The excerpt provides limited information relevant to thin-wall orientation effects in LPBF, but it does not specifically examine orientation relative to the recoater blade, shielding-gas flow direction, or position on the build plate. It does report that increasing wall inclination converts more of the wall into an overhang region, where the absence of solid substrate promotes more severe powder spattering and reduced successful deposition. Molten metal may infiltrate the powder bed and attach partially melted particles to the wall, although these particles were excluded from thickness measurements and did not contribute to wall strength. Inclined walls can also exhibit dimensional reduction because of staircase and infiltration effects. Regarding porosity, single-bead walls generally had low closed-porosity levels, while open pores could result from insufficient overlap between successive melt tracks. Increasing inclination makes track-to-track deviation more significant, potentially worsening this issue. Larger melt pools may reduce open porosity but can increase the risk of keyhole porosity. Rastered Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 thin walls showed substantial irregular pores associated with lack of fusion. The excerpt does not quantify powder-layer thickness variation near walls, recoating-induced deflection or swelling, gas-flow effects, or build-plate-location effects on porosity and melt-pool behavior.

The excerpt provides only indirect information relevant to LPBF thin-wall orientation and recoating effects. It explains that the EOS software changes from raster scanning with contour paths to single-bead scanning according to CAD wall thickness. The transition is approximately 300 μm for Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 and 350 μm for AlSi10Mg. Scan-path thickness depends on alloy and designed wall thickness, but not on inclination angle or processing parameters. Thin-wall distortion is identified as a major fabrication problem: Ti-6Al-4V walls distorted even with supports, while unsupported walls experienced more severe distortion and could cause build failure. The excerpt also notes that thin walls can accumulate more heat because the surrounding powder bed has low thermal conductivity, affecting melt-pool behavior and increasing keyholing risk when high-energy parameters are used. Low-energy parameters may reduce minimum wall dimensions but can produce insufficient melt-pool depth and inadequate remelting. However, this passage does not report experiments on wall orientation relative to the recoater blade or gas-flow direction, spatter deposition, recoating-induced swelling or deflection, local powder-layer thickness variation, or build-plate position effects on porosity and melt pools.

## pqac-00000037

From text 'choi2024opticalmicroscopyon pages 3-6'.

J. Choi, K. Zhou, E. Adcock, J. Pauza, A. Ngo, T. Swierzewski, J. Lewandowski, and A. Rollett. Optical microscopy on machined surfaces in ti-6al-4v reveals pore statistics that correlate with fatigue. IOP Conference Series: Materials Science and Engineering, 1310:012008, Aug 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1088/1757-899x/1310/1/012008, doi:10.1088/1757-899x/1310/1/012008. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt does not establish a minimum metallographic section area, volume, or number of pores required for statistically representative porosity measurement. Instead, it describes a surface-focused approach for LPBF Ti-6Al-4V fatigue specimens. The authors emphasize that optical microscopy and serial sectioning can detect thin “sliver” defects that may be missed by CT, particularly when defects are exposed at the machined surface. Their measurements were made on all four longitudinal planes of each bar to obtain a pore-size distribution intended to approach the bulk distribution, rather than relying on a single section. Approximately 500 microns were machined away, and the authors report minimal spatial variation in porosity in the resulting bars. For fatigue-relevant assessment, they separately analyzed pores within the maximum-tensile-stress region, approximately 10 × 5 mm, because this is the region from which cracks actually originate. This suggests that measurements should avoid interpreting only an edge or localized region and should instead use multiple faces and a defined interior/machined surface area. However, the excerpt gives no prescribed pore count, sampled volume, wall distance, or quantitative edge-exclusion rule for reliable porosity determination.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'zheng2021defectanalysisof pages 14-17'.

Zhi-Ping Zheng, L. Peng, and Di Wang. Defect analysis of 316 l stainless steel prepared by lpbf additive manufacturing processes. Coatings, 11:1562, Dec 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/coatings11121562, doi:10.3390/coatings11121562. This article has 34 citations.

The excerpt does not specify a minimum polished-section area, specimen volume, pore count, or statistical criterion required for a reliable porosity measurement. It describes one practical measurement approach: sample 2 was examined on a longitudinal polished section extending through the central part of the specimen along the Z-axis. Because the specimen was large, multiple 25× optical images were stitched together to analyze the entire tested area. The reported comparison used a single specimen and yielded densities of 96.30% by metallography and 97.00% by XCT, but these values do not establish a general statistically representative area or number of pores. The results demonstrate strong spatial variation and therefore indicate that edge or surface regions should not be treated as representative of the bulk. The top and bottom layers had more pores than the middle layer, while the layer nearest the nitrogen-contacting outer surface had the most pores; analogous trends occurred from the center toward the outer sides. For avoiding edge effects, measurements should therefore be taken in a central or middle region, away from the top, bottom, and outer side surfaces, while using a sufficiently large stitched area to capture the spatial distribution. A statistically defensible minimum would require additional sampling and a variance or convergence study, which is not provided here.

From text 'sola2019microstructuralporosityin pages 11-12'.

Antonella Sola and Alireza Nouri. Microstructural porosity in additive manufacturing: the formation and detection of pores in metal parts fabricated by powder bed fusion. Journal of Advanced Manufacturing and Processing, Jul 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.1002/amp2.10021, doi:10.1002/amp2.10021. This article has 526 citations.

The excerpt does not provide a minimum polished-section area, minimum analyzed volume, or required number of pores for statistically reliable porosity determination in an LPBF part. Instead, it emphasizes that microscopic porosity measurements lack a standardized imaging method and can be biased by magnification, focus, sampling location, and the number of images analyzed. For micro-CT, the appropriate representative volume depends on the balance between spatial resolution and the volume investigated: high resolution detects smaller pores but covers less material, while lower resolution covers larger volumes but misses small pores. The representative volume should therefore be selected based on the defect size and failure mechanism of interest. In fatigue-related evaluations, the excerpt states that the largest defect, rather than total pore-volume fraction, may control fatigue resistance, and that critical pores tend to be near the surface. Consequently, surface and subsurface regions should be deliberately included when assessing fatigue-critical porosity. This is not presented as a universal rule for avoiding metallographic edge effects, nor does the excerpt prescribe a central-wall sampling location or a fixed distance from edges. It also cautions that polished-section preparation can introduce artifacts and morphological changes.

The excerpt discusses island/sector scanning strategies generally, but it does not provide Concept Laser M2 software-specific behavior for narrow features or cross-sections smaller than one island. The reported island dimensions are 5 × 5 mm and 2.5 × 2.5 mm. Six strategies were compared, including sector patterns scanned successively or according to least heat influence. Sector/island strategies generally produced less deformation, and island scanning reduced curling angle; however, the cited experiment found that island section size did not influence curling angle. For vector length, the excerpt reports that reducing the bidirectional scan-vector length from 10 mm to 2 mm improved thermal stress by 13%. J. Elliott Fowler1     · Timothy J. Ruggles1 · Dale E. Cillessen2 · Kyle L. Johnson3 · Luis J. Jauregui1 · Robert L. Craig1 ·

Abstract
The need to optimize the processing conditions of additively manufactured (AM) metals and alloys has driven advances in
throughput capabilities for material property measurements such as tensile strength or hardness. High-throughput (HT) char-
acterization of AM metal microstructure has fallen significantly behind the pace of property measurements due to intrinsic
bottlenecks associated with the artisan and labor-intensive preparation methods required to produce highly polished surfaces.
This inequality in data throughput has led to a reliance on heuristics to connect process to structure or structure to properties
for AM structural materials. In this study, we show a transformative approach to achieve laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)
printing, HT preparation using dry electropolishing and HT electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). This approach was used
to construct a library of > 600 experimental EBSD sample sets spanning a diverse range of LPBF process conditions for
AM Kovar. This vast library is far more expansive in parameter space than most state-of-the-art studies, yet it required only
approximately 10 labor hours to acquire. Build geometries, surface preparation methods, and microscopy details, as well as
the entire library of >600 EBSD data sets over the two sample design versions, have been shared with intent for the materi-
als community to leverage the data and further advance the approach. Using this library, we investigated process–structure
relationships and uncovered an unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build, when varied,
using otherwise identical laser parameters.

## pqac-00000057

From text 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 5-7'.

Ziheng Wu, Sneha Prabha Narra, and Anthony Rollett. Exploring the fabrication limits of thin-wall structures in a laser powder bed fusion process. The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, 110:191-207, Aug 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4. This article has 241 citations.

The excerpt describes EOS software as selecting the scan strategy based on the thin wall’s CAD feature dimension. In raster mode, the interior is filled with short, parallel hatch vectors separated by the unit hatch spacing, followed by two contour scans intended to improve surface finish by remelting the solid–powder interface. When the feature is below the software’s transition thickness, it switches to single-bead mode: each layer is filled with one melt track and no contour scans are used. Thus, the narrow-wall strategy described here is not a contour-only mode; it is a single-bead mode for features below the threshold. The reported transition is approximately 300 μm for Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718, and approximately 350 μm for AlSi10Mg. The excerpt also notes that the scan-path thickness depends on alloy and is related to designed CAD wall thickness, while inclination angle and processing parameters do not affect scan-path thickness. The passage does not specify a universal “standard island size” threshold, but instead identifies the material-dependent CAD feature thickness at which raster/hatch scanning changes to single-bead scanning.


---

## pqac-00000058

From text 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 4-5'.

Ziheng Wu, Sneha Prabha Narra, and Anthony Rollett. Exploring the fabrication limits of thin-wall structures in a laser powder bed fusion process. The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, 110:191-207, Aug 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4. This article has 241 citations.

The excerpt indicates that EOS handles thin walls near the process-resolution limit by changing from raster scanning to single-bead scanning. In single-bead mode, the melt-pool width is the primary factor controlling the resulting wall thickness, and the authors use a Rosenthal analytical solution to select process parameters for a desired wall thickness. The excerpt also documents raster-mode fabrication using raster scans together with two contour settings, but it does not describe a separate “hatch with short vectors” strategy. It does not provide the standard island size, explain how walls narrower than that island size are specifically treated, or state a precise wall-thickness threshold at which the software switches modes. Table 1 lists tested single-bead target thicknesses of 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm for Ti-6Al-4V, 100 and 150 μm for Inconel 718, and 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm for AlSi10Mg. Table 2 separately lists raster and contour parameters for the materials. Thus, the excerpt supports a single-bead transition near the resolution limit, while the exact switching thickness and any Concept Laser behavior are not established here.

## pqac-00000059

From text 'wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 13-15'.

Ziheng Wu, Sneha Prabha Narra, and Anthony Rollett. Exploring the fabrication limits of thin-wall structures in a laser powder bed fusion process. The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology, 110:191-207, Aug 2020. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4. This article has 241 citations.

The excerpt does not describe how EOS or Concept Laser software handles walls narrower than a standard island size, nor does it mention contour-only scanning or hatch patterns with short vectors. It does, however, distinguish between single-bead and raster scan modes for thin walls fabricated on an EOS M290. Walls in the alloy-dependent “small size range” are beyond raster-mode capability and can only be fabricated using single-bead mode; their thickness is controlled primarily by melt-pool size rather than the CAD wall dimension. The stated small-wall thresholds are below 141 μm for Ti-6Al-4V, below 252 μm for Inconel 718, and below 146 μm for AlSi10Mg. Walls in the “medium size range” can be fabricated using either single-bead or raster modes, but single-bead mode is recommended because the raster path width is limited for small feature dimensions and may produce a pulse-welding pattern, unpredictable geometry, and unmelted regions. The excerpt therefore supplies alloy-specific transitions between raster and single-bead processing, but it does not establish a software rule involving island size, contour-only mode, or short hatch vectors.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "A summary table of the key risks and confounding factors when using ~1.3 mm thin LPBF walls for parameter screening compared with bulk material. The table should have columns: Issue, Mechanism, Direction of Effect on Porosity/Melt-Pool, Estimated Magnitude (with conditions), Mitigation, Key Reference(s). Include rows for: (1) Heat accumulation, (2) Short scan vectors/turnaround pores, (3) Contour-hatch interaction, (4) Recoater/gas flow orientation, (5) Spatter position dependence, (6) Measurement area limitations. Use the quantitative data from the evidence gathered, especially Mohr et al. 2020 (316L, SLM280, 275W/700mm/s short ILT 18s reaching 545\u00b0C, melt pool depth 13-19% increase, porosity up to 2.7%), Martin et al. 2019 (87% of pores within 200 \u00b5m of turnaround), Kim et al. 2021 (galvo limit ~10^6 mm/s\u00b2, 1.21 ms delay), du Plessis 2019 (0.05 mm offset creates contour porosity), Weaver et al. 2021 (3x4 mm combinatorial regions match bulk porosity <0.03%)."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Issue | Mechanism | Direction of Effect on Porosity/Melt-Pool | Estimated Magnitude (with conditions) | Mitigation | Key Reference(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heat accumulation | A small cross-section and surrounding low-conductivity powder restrict heat rejection; short inter-layer time (ILT), high energy input, increasing height, and fewer parts per layer raise the temperature before the next exposure. | Usually deeper/larger melt pools and greater keyhole risk; porosity may rise at high energy. The response is not universally monotonic because temperature-dependent Marangoni flow can make pools wider but shallower. | For 316L on an SLM280 HL in Ar with a 100 °C plate, 50 µm layers, 120 µm hatch, 275 W and 700 mm/s, the measured pre-exposure temperature reached about 545 °C at 18 s ILT, versus about 230 °C at 65 s and 170 °C at 116 s. Short versus intermediate ILT increased upper melt-pool depth by 13–19%; at 275 W, 560 mm/s and 18 s ILT, upper-section porosity reached 1.1–2.7%, versus 0.1–0.2% near the base. These values are bulk-cuboid evidence, not a direct prediction for a 7.6 mm wall. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000036) | Record actual layer/part exposure times; randomize parameter location and exposure order; include repeated controls across panels and positions; compare lower, middle, and upper wall regions; validate selected settings in bulk cubes; model the whole build’s transient thermal history rather than an isolated steady-state track. | Mohr et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080; Chaudry et al., 2022, DOI: 10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000036) |
| Short scan vectors / turnaround pores | In a roughly 1 mm-wide core, transverse vectors may spend a large fraction of their duration accelerating, decelerating, switching the laser, or turning. Reduced instantaneous speed raises local energy input and deepens the vapor depression; abrupt shutoff can collapse it and trap gas. Skywriting prevents exposure during acceleration only when galvo motion and laser timing are calibrated. | Turn regions can become locally deeper/keyholed and produce spherical pores; timing or following errors can instead truncate vectors and cause lack of fusion near the contour. Longitudinal 12.7 mm vectors should more closely approach steady state. | In synchrotron experiments, 87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turn; depression depth peaked about 100 µs after reversal and approached steady state after roughly 1000 µs. On the NIST AMMT, the calibrated galvo acceleration limit was approximately 10⁶ mm/s²; the measured command response was 1.26 ms, requiring a 1.21 ms position/power delay plus about 0.05 ms for laser rise. These machine-specific values must not be transferred directly to the Concept Laser M2. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048) | Extract and archive the actual CL WRX vectors, scan order, skywriting lengths, jump delays, and laser-on/off delays; compare transverse and longitudinal hatch separately; exclude or label the first/last approximately 0.2 mm of each vector when diagnosing bulk-like melt pools; calibrate endpoints on witness tracks; consider power ramping rather than abrupt on/off switching. | Martin et al., 2019, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2; Kim et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048) |
| Contour–hatch interaction | Slow, small-spot contours can penetrate deeply or keyhole; insufficient contour–hatch overlap leaves lack-of-fusion voids. Core vectors affected by galvo/timing error may stop before, or overshoot beyond, the intended interface. In a 1.27 mm wall, two contour/remelt zones occupy a substantial fraction of the width. | Adds interface-localized lack-of-fusion or keyhole pores and changes melt-pool geometry near both faces; nominally “core” porosity may therefore combine core, contour, and overlap behavior. | XCT experiments found near-edge contour porosity at a 0.05 mm hatch–contour offset, while the nominal 0.015 mm spacing did not show it; 0.03, 0.05, and 0.10 mm cases are compared in that paper’s Fig. 8. Other XCT work found small spherical/keyhole pores concentrated between perimeter and hatch. No primary study establishes a universal contour-free distance; a 0.2 mm face exclusion is plausible but unvalidated for the stated 50–70 µm contour spot and 130 µm core spot. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000045) | Map pore density versus distance from each face rather than imposing only one cutoff; measure contour and core melt-pool boundaries separately; document contour order and offset; retain unchanged contours for screening but validate finalists without contours or in much wider cubes to isolate the core response. | du Plessis, 2019, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871; Englert et al., 2022, DOI: 10.3390/ma15031105; Kim et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000046) |
| Recoater / gas-flow orientation | Tall, slender walls can distort, swell, or protrude into the recoater path; a wall crossing the recoater presents repeated leading-edge interactions, whereas a parallel wall may guide the blade along its length. Gas flow changes plume and spatter trajectories relative to the wall. | Recoater contact can deflect or damage walls and create local powder starvation, thick layers, or troughs, causing lack of fusion and dimensional scatter. Directional gas flow can create orientation-dependent redeposition, but the sign depends on machine flow topology and scan direction. | Thin-wall experiments document substantial distortion and possible build failure, but no reliable primary-source magnitude was found for parallel-versus-perpendicular 1.27 mm 316L walls on a Concept Laser M2. EOS evidence also shows that software can change scan mode below approximately 300–350 µm, but a 1.27 mm wall should remain rastered; Concept Laser behavior must be verified from actual build files. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000057) | Treat the 21 orientation pairs as a blocked experiment; record blade marks, recoater force/events, wall lean, width, and height; inspect layer images for streaks and powder depletion; report gas-flow direction independently of recoater direction; do not pool orientations until an equivalence test supports doing so. | Wu et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000057) |
| Spatter and plate-position dependence | Gas velocity and recirculation vary from inlet to outlet; particle trajectories depend on size, ejection angle, scan direction, and whether scanning is with or against the flow. Large or oxidized particles can be difficult to remelt and may disturb recoating. Off-axis laser incidence/focus can additionally alter spot shape and irradiance. | Redeposited spatter can cause local lack of fusion, roughness, and pore outliers; spatial gradients can masquerade as parameter effects. A simple monotonic increase toward the outlet is not established and should not be assumed. | Simulations show position- and strategy-dependent deposition and that larger particles deposit nearer the processing region; one SS316L simulation reported up to 72% overall spatter clearance at 1000 L/min, but this is not a Concept Laser M2 measurement. No quantitative M2-wide porosity gradient was found. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000056) | Include panel, x–y position, gas-flow coordinate, optical-axis distance, hatch direction, and exposure order as covariates; repeat controls at multiple locations; inspect and sieve powder after abnormal events; use plate maps and residual plots before attributing trends to P or v. | Cen et al., 2024, DOI: 10.1007/s00170-024-13596-7; Weaver et al., 2021, DOI: 10.6028/NIST.AMS.100-43. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056) |
| Measurement-area limitations | A single polished plane samples a small, geometry-dependent area; rare keyhole or lack-of-fusion defects create zero-inflated, high-variance estimates. Grinding can open or smear pores, and threshold choice changes measured area fraction. Excluding faces removes contour defects but also reduces the sampled core to only about 0.87 mm nominal width. | Mean porosity may appear artificially zero or fluctuate strongly between sections; the melt-pool depth in the last layer is especially sensitive to local scan direction, endpoint location, and polishing-plane alignment. | No universal minimum section area or pore count is standardized. A high-throughput IN625 study found less than 0.03% porosity in 3 × 4 mm combinatorial regions, comparable to a 20 × 20 mm regular sample, but warned that miniature and regular samples are not generally equivalent. Your nominal analysis window—approximately 0.87 mm × 5.6 mm, or 4.9 mm² after excluding 0.2 mm per face and 1 mm from base/top—is smaller than that comparison area and may contain very few pores in the dense regime. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | Report analyzed area, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, pore count, area fraction, and confidence/credible intervals; use multiple separated fields or serial sections; preserve full-wall maps so interface and core statistics can be reported separately; validate a subset by XCT and by wider bulk coupons; determine convergence by progressively enlarging the sampled area. | Weaver et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109969; Sola and Nouri, 2019, DOI: 10.1002/amp2.10021. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) |

function.arguments:
{"answer": "## Representativeness of Thin LPBF Walls for Bulk-Material Parameter Screening

### Overview

Thin walls (~1.3 mm) printed in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can provide useful relative rankings of process parameters but are subject to at least six systematic effects that can bias porosity and melt-pool depth relative to bulk material printed with the same P, v, hatch spacing, and layer thickness. The literature strongly supports the conclusion that **thin-wall results should be treated as screening data, not as absolute bulk-equivalent measurements**, and that finalist settings should be validated in wider cubes. The key confounders are summarized in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 1. Heat Accumulation in Thin Walls and Small Cross-Sections

Heat accumulation is the best-documented concern. In LPBF 316L stainless steel on an SLM 280 HL (single 400 W Yb fibre laser, Ar, 100 °C plate preheat, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, 275 W, 700 mm/s, VED ≈ 65 J/mm³), Mohr et al. measured a progressive rise in the pre-exposure (freshly recoated) surface temperature from ~100 °C at the base plate to ~545 °C at the top of a 114.5 mm cuboid when the inter-layer time (ILT) was only 18 s (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). At 65 s ILT the top reached ~230 °C, and at 116 s it was ~170 °C (pqac-00000032). These measurements were confirmed by a validated FEM model by Chaudry et al. (2022), which reproduced the layer-by-layer temperature rise to within ~7 °C for short ILT and ~30 °C for medium ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

The consequences for melt-pool depth and porosity are significant. Melt-pool depth in the upper section of the short-ILT cuboids was 13–19% larger than at intermediate or long ILT for the same VED (pqac-00000036). At 275 W, 560 mm/s (high VED, ~82 J/mm³) and 18 s ILT, porosity in the upper section reached 1.1–2.7% (mostly spherical keyhole pores), compared with 0.1–0.2% in the lower section and ≤0.3% at longer ILT (pqac-00000036). Sub-grain size also increased from 458 µm² (low VED) to 1386 µm² (high VED) for short ILT at the top of the build, while hardness dropped from 221 HV1 to 176 HV1 within the same specimen (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). These ILT-dependent effects were also correlated with the ratio of area exploitation (RAE): the short ILT of 18 s corresponded to an RAE of only ~1%, representative of a single small part on a large platform (pqac-00000036).

For the user's build, each thin wall (~1.27 × 12.7 mm cross-section, ~7.6 mm tall) has a very short per-layer exposure time, but each comb part has seven walls plus a base, and twelve combs share the build. The effective ILT therefore depends on how many walls and how many parts are scanned before the recoater returns—a quantity that the Concept Laser M2 controller determines from the exposure order and can vary with parameter set. With 12 combs and ~84 walls, the layer time should be moderate, but higher-power / lower-speed walls that take longer to scan will experience a different ILT than fast, low-power walls on the same layer.

Piazza et al. (2020) independently demonstrated on miniature 316L parts (60–70 W, 25 µm layers) that melt-pool depth decreased linearly with build height in both cylindrical and conical geometries, attributed to heat accumulation raising the substrate temperature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). They also confirmed that geometry affects the magnitude of the effect: the cross-sectional-area variation in a cone produced lower overall porosity than in a constant-section cylinder, because conical layers conduct heat differently (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for 316L on SLM 280 HL; directly applicable in principle but quantitatively transferable to the Concept Laser M2 only with caution (different optics, chamber flow, build strategy). The referenced data are in Mohr et al. (2020, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080, Figs. 3, 7, 8, Table 1) and Chaudry et al. (2022, doi:10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x, Figs. 10, 12, 13).

---

### 2. Short Hatch Vectors, Scanner Turnaround, and Skywriting

In a ~1 mm-wide core (after contour exclusion), transverse hatch vectors are approximately 1 mm long. Each vector spends a large fraction of its duration in the acceleration and deceleration zones of the galvanometer mirrors. Martin et al. (2019) used in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging at 316L-relevant conditions to show that during turnaround, the vapor depression deepens as the galvanometer decelerates and the laser lingers near-stationary. The depression peaked approximately 100 µs after the reversal and approached steady state only after ~1000 µs. As the scanner accelerated away into a pre-heated region, the depression rapidly collapsed and trapped gas, creating spherical pores. In their experiments, **87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turnaround point** (pqac-00000004). At a programmed speed of 1000 mm/s, 89% of pores formed in under 500 µs (pqac-00000002).

**Skywriting** (turning the laser off at the end of each vector so that it does not expose the turnaround) does not reliably eliminate these pores: the abrupt transition from keyhole-mode exposure to zero power causes its own rapid depression collapse and can produce an end-of-track pore (pqac-00000003). The proposed mitigation is smooth, controlled power modulation that avoids keyhole formation and prevents rapid pressure changes in the melt pool (pqac-00000003).

Kim et al. (2021) systematically varied galvanometer acceleration and laser on/off delay on the NIST AMMT (IN625, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, 40 µm layers) and characterized the resulting pores by XCT. They identified two types of error: **following error** (galvo cannot physically follow the commanded acceleration, so actual track positions drift inward and do not reach the contour) and **synchronization error** (laser power switches too early or too late relative to galvo position). The galvo acceleration limit for the AMMT was ~10⁶ mm/s², and the calibrated position/power delay was 1.21 ms (plus ~0.05 ms for the laser to reach full power) (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). With a 50× higher commanded acceleration, tracks oscillated within the core and never reached the contour, leaving an annular lack-of-fusion zone (pqac-00000048). Revanur (2024) separately reports pipeline delays of 250–500 µs and point-exposure delays of 10–50 µs in LPBF galvo systems (pqac-00000007).

For the user's build, a ~1 mm transverse vector at ~1350 mm/s requires only ~0.74 ms of steady travel—comparable to the total galvo response/delay budget. The fraction of each vector spent in acceleration/deceleration transients is therefore much larger than in a 12.7 mm longitudinal vector. This means transverse-vector layers will have more turnaround-related defects per unit volume than longitudinal-vector layers. The Concept Laser island scanning strategy (5 × 5 mm islands, vectors rotated 90° between adjacent islands, islands shifted between layers) further multiplies turnaround events (pqac-00000041). At 1.27 mm wall width, the core is narrower than a standard island, so the software must either assign a single stripe or treat the wall as a narrow feature. The exact behavior should be verified from the exported build file or CL WRX logs.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong (Martin et al. 2019, doi:10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2, in Nature Communications with 922 citations; Kim et al. 2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372). Machine-specific galvo and delay parameters are not transferable from the AMMT to the Concept Laser M2, but the physics is universal.

---

### 3. Contour–Hatch Interaction

In the user's build, contours at 100–120 W and 130–220 mm/s with a 50–70 µm spot produce P/v ≈ 0.45–0.92 J/mm—substantially higher linear energy density than the core hatch P/v = 0.274 J/mm at the production setting. The focused, slow contour is therefore more likely to operate in keyhole mode, and the contour–core interface is a known location for porosity.

Du Plessis (2019) studied 316L (EOS parameters, XCT) and found that increasing the hatch-to-contour offset from the nominal 0.015 mm to 0.05 mm introduced visible subsurface porosity near the part edges; at 0.10 mm offset the porosity was severe (pqac-00000017). Englert et al. (2022) found, in their XCT analysis of hatching versus concentric strategies, that keyhole pores were concentrated specifically between the perimeter and the hatching region (pqac-00000018). Kim et al. (2021) described near-surface pores close to the contour–core boundary, attributing them in part to laser control errors (following and synchronization errors) that truncate or extend tracks at the interface (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

In a 1.27 mm wall, contour regions on both faces may each penetrate ~0.1–0.2 mm inward (melt-pool half-width plus heat-affected zone), consuming 0.2–0.4 mm of the total width. After excluding 0.2 mm from each face, the remaining core window is only ~0.87 mm wide. This is narrow enough that contour-induced thermal effects (preheating, remelting, keyhole remnants) may still reach the center, especially at higher contour powers. No primary source was found that quantifies the exact contour-free depth for the stated parameters; the user should map pore density as a function of distance from each face to establish this empirically.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The mechanism is well supported, but quantitative width of the contour-affected zone has not been reported for the specific Concept Laser M2 parameters. Key references: du Plessis (2019, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871, Fig. 8) and Kim et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372).

---

### 4. Published High-Throughput Parameter Screening with Miniature Specimens

The closest published precedent is the NIST combinatorial LPBF approach by Weaver et al. (2021), who built a single specimen of IN625 containing 24 columns of 4 mm × 3 mm cross-section, each with a different combination of five laser powers and four scan speeds (60 unique conditions with post-processing variants). Porosity in the miniature combinatorial regions was below 0.03%, comparable to that of a larger 20 × 20 mm regular sample (pqac-00000013). However, hardness was lower in the combinatorial regions, indicating a geometry or thermal-history effect, and **the authors explicitly cautioned that combinatorial-sample information is not equivalent to regular-sample information and that validation against bulk specimens is necessary** (pqac-00000014). They recommended thicker porous dividers or unmelted-powder gaps between regions to reduce inter-column thermal coupling.

Fowler et al. (2024) at Sandia National Laboratories used 3 × 3 × 3 mm Kovar (Fe-29Ni-17Co) cubes in linear arrays on a Renishaw AM400 (50 µm layers), with 100–200 unique parameter sets per build plate, and characterized them by automated EBSD after surface grinding and dry electropolishing. They uncovered an **unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build** even for identical laser parameters (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This finding underscores that plate-position effects (thermal environment, gas flow, spatter) can be as important as the intentionally varied parameters and must be blocked or randomized.

Agrawal and Thoma (2022) demonstrated high-throughput surface characterization for 316L process screening, turning off contour and upskin parameters to isolate core behavior. The user's choice to keep contours fixed is a defensible alternative but adds the contour-interaction confound discussed above.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for the conclusion that miniature specimens can rank parameters, but moderate-to-weak for the claim that they reproduce absolute bulk density. Weaver et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109969, Figs. and Tables therein) is the most directly relevant reference.

---

### 5. Orientation Relative to Recoater and Gas Flow

The user's fourth panel is rotated 90° so that walls run across the recoater rather than along it, repeating 18 settings plus the control. This is a valuable blocking strategy. Several mechanisms can produce orientation-dependent results:

- **Recoater collision.** Tall, narrow walls that distort or swell above the powder plane can interfere with the recoater blade. Ti-6Al-4V thin walls showed substantial distortion even with supports, and unsupported walls could cause build failure (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). Walls perpendicular to the recoater present a leading edge on every stroke, while parallel walls may guide the blade along their length. The resulting powder-layer thickness variation can be asymmetric around the wall.

- **Gas-flow direction.** Spatter ejected from the melt pool is preferentially transported by the cross-flow. When scanning is opposite to the gas flow, larger particles decelerate and may redeposit on the same or adjacent walls; when aligned, spatter is more effectively carried away (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Gas velocity decreases from inlet to outlet, creating a spatial gradient of spatter deposition and plume interaction (pqac-00000050). No primary study was found that quantitatively compares porosity in thin walls parallel versus perpendicular to the recoater or gas flow for 316L on a Concept Laser M2.

- **Plate-position and optical effects.** Laser incidence angle, focus offset, and spot ellipticity vary with distance from the optical axis. These can alter melt-pool depth and width systematically across the plate. The Fowler et al. (2024) observation of location-dependent microstructure at identical parameters is consistent with such effects (pqac-00000043).

**Strength of evidence:** Mechanistic reasoning is strong, but quantitative orientation-specific data for the user's geometry and machine are absent. The user's paired-orientation design is itself a valuable contribution to the field. Key reference: Wu et al. (2020, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4).

---

### 6. Minimum Wall Thickness and Measurement Area for Porosity

No universally standardized minimum section area, pore count, or sampling protocol exists for LPBF metallographic porosity (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). Sola and Nouri (2019) emphasize that microscopic porosity measurements lack standardized imaging methods and are biased by magnification, focus, sampling location, and the number of images analyzed (pqac-00000039). Shahabi et al. (2022, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2022.112027) developed a statistical framework for determining data requirements for porosity characterization in LPBF; this paper was unobtainable for detailed review but is the key primary reference for this question.

In the user's design, after excluding 0.2 mm from each face and 1 mm from the top and bottom, the analysis window in each wall is approximately 0.87 mm × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm². This is comparable to but smaller than the 3 × 4 mm = 12 mm² regions used by Weaver et al. (2021), where porosity was <0.03% (pqac-00000013). In the dense regime (<0.1%), a 4.9 mm² section at SEM resolution (sub-micrometer pixels) may contain only a few countable pores, making the area-fraction estimate highly uncertain. At higher porosity (>0.5%), the section may contain enough pores for a reasonable estimate.

Choi et al. (2024) addressed this by measuring all four longitudinal machined faces of Ti-6Al-4V fatigue bars, noting that multiple faces approach the bulk pore-size distribution better than a single section (pqac-00000037). For the user's walls, measuring both halves of the bisected wall (mirror sections) would double the sampled area.

**Practical guidance:** The user's exclusion zones (0.2 mm from faces, 1 mm from base and top) are reasonable but should be justified empirically by plotting pore density versus distance from each boundary. The 0.2 mm face exclusion should be verified against the actual contour melt-pool boundary. All reported porosity values should include the analyzed area, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, number of pores detected, and a confidence interval (e.g., Clopper–Pearson or bootstrap). Convergence can be assessed by progressively enlarging the analysis window and observing stability.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The statistical framework exists (Shahabi et al. 2022) but was not fully reviewed. The qualitative guidance is well supported by multiple sources. Key additional reference: Sola and Nouri (2019, doi:10.1002/amp2.10021).

---

### Summary Assessment

Thin LPBF walls of ~1.3 mm thickness can serve as an efficient screening tool for ranking process parameters by porosity and melt-pool depth, as demonstrated by analogous miniature-specimen approaches (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000043). However, they are **not** unconditionally representative of bulk material because:

1. **Heat accumulation** raises the temperature of thin, tall features and shifts the melt-pool regime toward deeper/wider pools and potentially into keyhole porosity—especially at high P/v and short ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).
2. **Short scan vectors** in a ~1 mm core compress the steady-state fraction of each track and amplify turnaround-pore mechanisms (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).
3. **Contour–core overlap** occupies a significant fraction of the 1.27 mm width, mixing contour and core porosity signatures (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000045).
4. **Orientation and position on the plate** introduce systematic biases from recoater interaction, gas-flow-dependent spatter, and optical-axis effects (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000049).
5. **Small measurement area** limits the statistical precision of porosity estimates in the dense regime (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000013).

The user's experimental design already incorporates several strong mitigations: scrambled Sobol sampling, repeated controls, two orientations, and SEM imaging. Additional recommended steps include (a) archiving the actual CL WRX scan files so that vector lengths, exposure order, and ILT can be reconstructed; (b) mapping pore density versus distance from each face to identify the contour-free zone; (c) comparing the production-set control walls with the production-set base blocks; and (d) validating finalist settings in wider (≥10 × 10 mm) density cubes before using the results to calibrate the Thermo-Calc AM Module or to seed Bayesian optimization."}
