{"answer": "## Representativeness of Thin LPBF Walls for Bulk-Material Parameter Screening

### Overview

Thin walls (~1.3 mm) printed in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can provide useful relative rankings of process parameters but are subject to at least six systematic effects that can bias porosity and melt-pool depth relative to bulk material printed with the same P, v, hatch spacing, and layer thickness. The literature strongly supports the conclusion that **thin-wall results should be treated as screening data, not as absolute bulk-equivalent measurements**, and that finalist settings should be validated in wider cubes. The key confounders are summarized in the following table:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 1. Heat Accumulation in Thin Walls and Small Cross-Sections

Heat accumulation is the best-documented concern. In LPBF 316L stainless steel on an SLM 280 HL (single 400 W Yb fibre laser, Ar, 100 °C plate preheat, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, 275 W, 700 mm/s, VED ≈ 65 J/mm³), Mohr et al. measured a progressive rise in the pre-exposure (freshly recoated) surface temperature from ~100 °C at the base plate to ~545 °C at the top of a 114.5 mm cuboid when the inter-layer time (ILT) was only 18 s (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). At 65 s ILT the top reached ~230 °C, and at 116 s it was ~170 °C (pqac-00000032). These measurements were confirmed by a validated FEM model by Chaudry et al. (2022), which reproduced the layer-by-layer temperature rise to within ~7 °C for short ILT and ~30 °C for medium ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

The consequences for melt-pool depth and porosity are significant. Melt-pool depth in the upper section of the short-ILT cuboids was 13–19% larger than at intermediate or long ILT for the same VED (pqac-00000036). At 275 W, 560 mm/s (high VED, ~82 J/mm³) and 18 s ILT, porosity in the upper section reached 1.1–2.7% (mostly spherical keyhole pores), compared with 0.1–0.2% in the lower section and ≤0.3% at longer ILT (pqac-00000036). Sub-grain size also increased from 458 µm² (low VED) to 1386 µm² (high VED) for short ILT at the top of the build, while hardness dropped from 221 HV1 to 176 HV1 within the same specimen (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). These ILT-dependent effects were also correlated with the ratio of area exploitation (RAE): the short ILT of 18 s corresponded to an RAE of only ~1%, representative of a single small part on a large platform (pqac-00000036).

For the user's build, each thin wall (~1.27 × 12.7 mm cross-section, ~7.6 mm tall) has a very short per-layer exposure time, but each comb part has seven walls plus a base, and twelve combs share the build. The effective ILT therefore depends on how many walls and how many parts are scanned before the recoater returns—a quantity that the Concept Laser M2 controller determines from the exposure order and can vary with parameter set. With 12 combs and ~84 walls, the layer time should be moderate, but higher-power / lower-speed walls that take longer to scan will experience a different ILT than fast, low-power walls on the same layer.

Piazza et al. (2020) independently demonstrated on miniature 316L parts (60–70 W, 25 µm layers) that melt-pool depth decreased linearly with build height in both cylindrical and conical geometries, attributed to heat accumulation raising the substrate temperature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). They also confirmed that geometry affects the magnitude of the effect: the cross-sectional-area variation in a cone produced lower overall porosity than in a constant-section cylinder, because conical layers conduct heat differently (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for 316L on SLM 280 HL; directly applicable in principle but quantitatively transferable to the Concept Laser M2 only with caution (different optics, chamber flow, build strategy). The referenced data are in Mohr et al. (2020, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080, Figs. 3, 7, 8, Table 1) and Chaudry et al. (2022, doi:10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x, Figs. 10, 12, 13).

---

### 2. Short Hatch Vectors, Scanner Turnaround, and Skywriting

In a ~1 mm-wide core (after contour exclusion), transverse hatch vectors are approximately 1 mm long. Each vector spends a large fraction of its duration in the acceleration and deceleration zones of the galvanometer mirrors. Martin et al. (2019) used in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging at 316L-relevant conditions to show that during turnaround, the vapor depression deepens as the galvanometer decelerates and the laser lingers near-stationary. The depression peaked approximately 100 µs after the reversal and approached steady state only after ~1000 µs. As the scanner accelerated away into a pre-heated region, the depression rapidly collapsed and trapped gas, creating spherical pores. In their experiments, **87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turnaround point** (pqac-00000004). At a programmed speed of 1000 mm/s, 89% of pores formed in under 500 µs (pqac-00000002).

**Skywriting** (turning the laser off at the end of each vector so that it does not expose the turnaround) does not reliably eliminate these pores: the abrupt transition from keyhole-mode exposure to zero power causes its own rapid depression collapse and can produce an end-of-track pore (pqac-00000003). The proposed mitigation is smooth, controlled power modulation that avoids keyhole formation and prevents rapid pressure changes in the melt pool (pqac-00000003).

Kim et al. (2021) systematically varied galvanometer acceleration and laser on/off delay on the NIST AMMT (IN625, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, 40 µm layers) and characterized the resulting pores by XCT. They identified two types of error: **following error** (galvo cannot physically follow the commanded acceleration, so actual track positions drift inward and do not reach the contour) and **synchronization error** (laser power switches too early or too late relative to galvo position). The galvo acceleration limit for the AMMT was ~10⁶ mm/s², and the calibrated position/power delay was 1.21 ms (plus ~0.05 ms for the laser to reach full power) (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). With a 50× higher commanded acceleration, tracks oscillated within the core and never reached the contour, leaving an annular lack-of-fusion zone (pqac-00000048). Revanur (2024) separately reports pipeline delays of 250–500 µs and point-exposure delays of 10–50 µs in LPBF galvo systems (pqac-00000007).

For the user's build, a ~1 mm transverse vector at ~1350 mm/s requires only ~0.74 ms of steady travel—comparable to the total galvo response/delay budget. The fraction of each vector spent in acceleration/deceleration transients is therefore much larger than in a 12.7 mm longitudinal vector. This means transverse-vector layers will have more turnaround-related defects per unit volume than longitudinal-vector layers. The Concept Laser island scanning strategy (5 × 5 mm islands, vectors rotated 90° between adjacent islands, islands shifted between layers) further multiplies turnaround events (pqac-00000041). At 1.27 mm wall width, the core is narrower than a standard island, so the software must either assign a single stripe or treat the wall as a narrow feature. The exact behavior should be verified from the exported build file or CL WRX logs.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong (Martin et al. 2019, doi:10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2, in Nature Communications with 922 citations; Kim et al. 2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372). Machine-specific galvo and delay parameters are not transferable from the AMMT to the Concept Laser M2, but the physics is universal.

---

### 3. Contour–Hatch Interaction

In the user's build, contours at 100–120 W and 130–220 mm/s with a 50–70 µm spot produce P/v ≈ 0.45–0.92 J/mm—substantially higher linear energy density than the core hatch P/v = 0.274 J/mm at the production setting. The focused, slow contour is therefore more likely to operate in keyhole mode, and the contour–core interface is a known location for porosity.

Du Plessis (2019) studied 316L (EOS parameters, XCT) and found that increasing the hatch-to-contour offset from the nominal 0.015 mm to 0.05 mm introduced visible subsurface porosity near the part edges; at 0.10 mm offset the porosity was severe (pqac-00000017). Englert et al. (2022) found, in their XCT analysis of hatching versus concentric strategies, that keyhole pores were concentrated specifically between the perimeter and the hatching region (pqac-00000018). Kim et al. (2021) described near-surface pores close to the contour–core boundary, attributing them in part to laser control errors (following and synchronization errors) that truncate or extend tracks at the interface (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

In a 1.27 mm wall, contour regions on both faces may each penetrate ~0.1–0.2 mm inward (melt-pool half-width plus heat-affected zone), consuming 0.2–0.4 mm of the total width. After excluding 0.2 mm from each face, the remaining core window is only ~0.87 mm wide. This is narrow enough that contour-induced thermal effects (preheating, remelting, keyhole remnants) may still reach the center, especially at higher contour powers. No primary source was found that quantifies the exact contour-free depth for the stated parameters; the user should map pore density as a function of distance from each face to establish this empirically.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The mechanism is well supported, but quantitative width of the contour-affected zone has not been reported for the specific Concept Laser M2 parameters. Key references: du Plessis (2019, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871, Fig. 8) and Kim et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372).

---

### 4. Published High-Throughput Parameter Screening with Miniature Specimens

The closest published precedent is the NIST combinatorial LPBF approach by Weaver et al. (2021), who built a single specimen of IN625 containing 24 columns of 4 mm × 3 mm cross-section, each with a different combination of five laser powers and four scan speeds (60 unique conditions with post-processing variants). Porosity in the miniature combinatorial regions was below 0.03%, comparable to that of a larger 20 × 20 mm regular sample (pqac-00000013). However, hardness was lower in the combinatorial regions, indicating a geometry or thermal-history effect, and **the authors explicitly cautioned that combinatorial-sample information is not equivalent to regular-sample information and that validation against bulk specimens is necessary** (pqac-00000014). They recommended thicker porous dividers or unmelted-powder gaps between regions to reduce inter-column thermal coupling.

Fowler et al. (2024) at Sandia National Laboratories used 3 × 3 × 3 mm Kovar (Fe-29Ni-17Co) cubes in linear arrays on a Renishaw AM400 (50 µm layers), with 100–200 unique parameter sets per build plate, and characterized them by automated EBSD after surface grinding and dry electropolishing. They uncovered an **unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build** even for identical laser parameters (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This finding underscores that plate-position effects (thermal environment, gas flow, spatter) can be as important as the intentionally varied parameters and must be blocked or randomized.

Agrawal and Thoma (2022) demonstrated high-throughput surface characterization for 316L process screening, turning off contour and upskin parameters to isolate core behavior. The user's choice to keep contours fixed is a defensible alternative but adds the contour-interaction confound discussed above.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for the conclusion that miniature specimens can rank parameters, but moderate-to-weak for the claim that they reproduce absolute bulk density. Weaver et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109969, Figs. and Tables therein) is the most directly relevant reference.

---

### 5. Orientation Relative to Recoater and Gas Flow

The user's fourth panel is rotated 90° so that walls run across the recoater rather than along it, repeating 18 settings plus the control. This is a valuable blocking strategy. Several mechanisms can produce orientation-dependent results:

- **Recoater collision.** Tall, narrow walls that distort or swell above the powder plane can interfere with the recoater blade. Ti-6Al-4V thin walls showed substantial distortion even with supports, and unsupported walls could cause build failure (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). Walls perpendicular to the recoater present a leading edge on every stroke, while parallel walls may guide the blade along their length. The resulting powder-layer thickness variation can be asymmetric around the wall.

- **Gas-flow direction.** Spatter ejected from the melt pool is preferentially transported by the cross-flow. When scanning is opposite to the gas flow, larger particles decelerate and may redeposit on the same or adjacent walls; when aligned, spatter is more effectively carried away (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Gas velocity decreases from inlet to outlet, creating a spatial gradient of spatter deposition and plume interaction (pqac-00000050). No primary study was found that quantitatively compares porosity in thin walls parallel versus perpendicular to the recoater or gas flow for 316L on a Concept Laser M2.

- **Plate-position and optical effects.** Laser incidence angle, focus offset, and spot ellipticity vary with distance from the optical axis. These can alter melt-pool depth and width systematically across the plate. The Fowler et al. (2024) observation of location-dependent microstructure at identical parameters is consistent with such effects (pqac-00000043).

**Strength of evidence:** Mechanistic reasoning is strong, but quantitative orientation-specific data for the user's geometry and machine are absent. The user's paired-orientation design is itself a valuable contribution to the field. Key reference: Wu et al. (2020, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4).

---

### 6. Minimum Wall Thickness and Measurement Area for Porosity

No universally standardized minimum section area, pore count, or sampling protocol exists for LPBF metallographic porosity (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). Sola and Nouri (2019) emphasize that microscopic porosity measurements lack standardized imaging methods and are biased by magnification, focus, sampling location, and the number of images analyzed (pqac-00000039). Shahabi et al. (2022, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2022.112027) developed a statistical framework for determining data requirements for porosity characterization in LPBF; this paper was unobtainable for detailed review but is the key primary reference for this question.

In the user's design, after excluding 0.2 mm from each face and 1 mm from the top and bottom, the analysis window in each wall is approximately 0.87 mm × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm². This is comparable to but smaller than the 3 × 4 mm = 12 mm² regions used by Weaver et al. (2021), where porosity was <0.03% (pqac-00000013). In the dense regime (<0.1%), a 4.9 mm² section at SEM resolution (sub-micrometer pixels) may contain only a few countable pores, making the area-fraction estimate highly uncertain. At higher porosity (>0.5%), the section may contain enough pores for a reasonable estimate.

Choi et al. (2024) addressed this by measuring all four longitudinal machined faces of Ti-6Al-4V fatigue bars, noting that multiple faces approach the bulk pore-size distribution better than a single section (pqac-00000037). For the user's walls, measuring both halves of the bisected wall (mirror sections) would double the sampled area.

**Practical guidance:** The user's exclusion zones (0.2 mm from faces, 1 mm from base and top) are reasonable but should be justified empirically by plotting pore density versus distance from each boundary. The 0.2 mm face exclusion should be verified against the actual contour melt-pool boundary. All reported porosity values should include the analyzed area, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, number of pores detected, and a confidence interval (e.g., Clopper–Pearson or bootstrap). Convergence can be assessed by progressively enlarging the analysis window and observing stability.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The statistical framework exists (Shahabi et al. 2022) but was not fully reviewed. The qualitative guidance is well supported by multiple sources. Key additional reference: Sola and Nouri (2019, doi:10.1002/amp2.10021).

---

### Summary Assessment

Thin LPBF walls of ~1.3 mm thickness can serve as an efficient screening tool for ranking process parameters by porosity and melt-pool depth, as demonstrated by analogous miniature-specimen approaches (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000043). However, they are **not** unconditionally representative of bulk material because:

1. **Heat accumulation** raises the temperature of thin, tall features and shifts the melt-pool regime toward deeper/wider pools and potentially into keyhole porosity—especially at high P/v and short ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).
2. **Short scan vectors** in a ~1 mm core compress the steady-state fraction of each track and amplify turnaround-pore mechanisms (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).
3. **Contour–core overlap** occupies a significant fraction of the 1.27 mm width, mixing contour and core porosity signatures (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000045).
4. **Orientation and position on the plate** introduce systematic biases from recoater interaction, gas-flow-dependent spatter, and optical-axis effects (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000049).
5. **Small measurement area** limits the statistical precision of porosity estimates in the dense regime (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000013).

The user's experimental design already incorporates several strong mitigations: scrambled Sobol sampling, repeated controls, two orientations, and SEM imaging. Additional recommended steps include (a) archiving the actual CL WRX scan files so that vector lengths, exposure order, and ILT can be reconstructed; (b) mapping pore density versus distance from each face to identify the contour-free zone; (c) comparing the production-set control walls with the production-set base blocks; and (d) validating finalist settings in wider (≥10 × 10 mm) density cubes before using the results to calibrate the Thermo-Calc AM Module or to seed Bayesian optimization."}

state.question:
Do thin LPBF walls about 1.3 mm thick, each printed with its own core laser power and scan speed inside standard contours, give porosity and melt-pool depth that represent bulk material printed with the same parameters? What changes in a thin wall, and what can go wrong? Context: laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M, L-PBF) of commercial gas-atomized 316L stainless steel powder (about 15-45 um) on a Concept Laser M2 cusing (CL WRX Control 2.4; two 400 W class continuous-wave Yb fibre lasers at about 1070 nm, only one used; galvanometer scanner; nitrogen or argon; no plate heating; layer thickness 30 or 50 um, not yet confirmed). The machine's production 316L parameter set uses, for the core hatch, 370 W, 1350 mm/s, 0.09 mm hatch spacing and a 130 um spot (P/v = 0.274 J/mm), contours at 100-120 W and 130-220 mm/s with a 50-70 um spot, and an upskin at 200 W, 980 mm/s, 0.075 mm hatch. The build: 12 'comb' parts, each a 44.5 x 12.7 mm base (printed with the production set) carrying 7 thin walls (fins) 1.27 mm thick, 12.7 mm long and 7.6 mm tall on a 7.2 mm pitch. Every wall has its own core and upskin laser power P and scan speed v (contours unchanged): 60 settings from a scrambled Sobol sequence over P = 150-370 W and P/v = 0.09-0.55 J/mm (v about 335-2930 mm/s; about 33-204 J/mm^3 at 30 um layers), plus the production hatch as a control. Three parts stand on each of four removable 88 mm square 316L panels; the fourth panel is turned 90 degrees so its walls run across the recoater instead of along it, and repeats 18 settings and the control, giving 21 pairs printed in both orientations. After the build each part is cut lengthwise near its centreline and between walls 4 and 5, hot-mounted in 1.25 in conductive mounts, ground to the centreline (a section through every wall's thickness and height at mid-length), polished, imaged unetched in an SEM (Thermo Fisher Apreo C) for porosity in each wall's core (at least 0.2 mm from the faces, 1 mm from the base and the top), then etched to reveal the last layer's melt-pool boundaries. The results will be compared with the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing (AM) Module (CALPHAD-based properties; steady-state and transient melt-pool calculations; printability maps of lack of fusion, keyholing and balling), to calibrate and test it, and later builds will choose settings by batch Bayesian optimization.

Answer with citations and DOIs. Quote numbers with the conditions they apply to (material, P, v, spot size and how it was defined, hatch spacing, layer thickness, machine, gas). Prefer primary sources, say where sources disagree, and flag which statements are strongly versus weakly supported. Where a paper gives a data table or an open dataset we could compare against, say exactly where (table or figure number, repository and identifier).

In particular:
1. Heat accumulation in thin walls and small cross-sections: measured or simulated temperature rise layer by layer, its effect on melt-pool depth and porosity, and how it depends on wall thickness, height, P/v, layer time and the number of parts per layer.
2. Short hatch vectors: if the hatch runs across a 1 mm wide core, every vector is about 1 mm long; how scanner acceleration, turnaround, skywriting and laser on/off delays change porosity (turnaround pores) and melt-pool depth; versus vectors along a 12.7 mm wall. Concept Laser's island scanning strategy and how it treats a narrow part.
3. Contour and hatch interaction: porosity near the contour-hatch interface, keyhole pores from slow, focused contour scans, and how far inside the faces the core is free of contour effects.
4. Published high-throughput parameter screening with thin walls, fins, combs, stepped or 'tree' specimens, pins or small cubes on one plate: how well the result matched bulk density cubes.
5. Orientation of thin walls to the recoater and to the gas flow: recoater collision, wall deflection or swelling, powder-layer thickness next to walls, spatter landing; effects of the part's position on the plate (gas-flow inlet to outlet, distance from the laser's optical axis, angle of incidence, focus) on porosity and melt-pool size.
6. Minimum wall thickness and height for a meaningful porosity measurement in a polished section, and where in the wall to measure.

## Representativeness of Thin LPBF Walls for Bulk-Material Parameter Screening

### Overview

Thin walls (~1.3 mm) printed in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can provide useful relative rankings of process parameters but are subject to at least six systematic effects that can bias porosity and melt-pool depth relative to bulk material printed with the same P, v, hatch spacing, and layer thickness. The literature strongly supports the conclusion that **thin-wall results should be treated as screening data, not as absolute bulk-equivalent measurements**, and that finalist settings should be validated in wider cubes. The key confounders are summarized in the following table:

| Issue | Mechanism | Direction of Effect on Porosity/Melt-Pool | Estimated Magnitude (with conditions) | Mitigation | Key Reference(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heat accumulation | A small cross-section and surrounding low-conductivity powder restrict heat rejection; short inter-layer time (ILT), high energy input, increasing height, and fewer parts per layer raise the temperature before the next exposure. | Usually deeper/larger melt pools and greater keyhole risk; porosity may rise at high energy. The response is not universally monotonic because temperature-dependent Marangoni flow can make pools wider but shallower. | For 316L on an SLM280 HL in Ar with a 100 °C plate, 50 µm layers, 120 µm hatch, 275 W and 700 mm/s, the measured pre-exposure temperature reached about 545 °C at 18 s ILT, versus about 230 °C at 65 s and 170 °C at 116 s. Short versus intermediate ILT increased upper melt-pool depth by 13–19%; at 275 W, 560 mm/s and 18 s ILT, upper-section porosity reached 1.1–2.7%, versus 0.1–0.2% near the base. These values are bulk-cuboid evidence, not a direct prediction for a 7.6 mm wall. (chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 7-9, chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 9-10, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 3-4, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9) | Record actual layer/part exposure times; randomize parameter location and exposure order; include repeated controls across panels and positions; compare lower, middle, and upper wall regions; validate selected settings in bulk cubes; model the whole build’s transient thermal history rather than an isolated steady-state track. | Mohr et al., 2020, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080; Chaudry et al., 2022, DOI: 10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x. (chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 7-9, chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 9-10, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9) |
| Short scan vectors / turnaround pores | In a roughly 1 mm-wide core, transverse vectors may spend a large fraction of their duration accelerating, decelerating, switching the laser, or turning. Reduced instantaneous speed raises local energy input and deepens the vapor depression; abrupt shutoff can collapse it and trap gas. Skywriting prevents exposure during acceleration only when galvo motion and laser timing are calibrated. | Turn regions can become locally deeper/keyholed and produce spherical pores; timing or following errors can instead truncate vectors and cause lack of fusion near the contour. Longitudinal 12.7 mm vectors should more closely approach steady state. | In synchrotron experiments, 87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turn; depression depth peaked about 100 µs after reversal and approached steady state after roughly 1000 µs. On the NIST AMMT, the calibrated galvo acceleration limit was approximately 10⁶ mm/s²; the measured command response was 1.26 ms, requiring a 1.21 ms position/power delay plus about 0.05 ms for laser rise. These machine-specific values must not be transferred directly to the Concept Laser M2. (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 4-4, martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 6-6, martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 1-2, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 6-7, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 7-9) | Extract and archive the actual CL WRX vectors, scan order, skywriting lengths, jump delays, and laser-on/off delays; compare transverse and longitudinal hatch separately; exclude or label the first/last approximately 0.2 mm of each vector when diagnosing bulk-like melt pools; calibrate endpoints on witness tracks; consider power ramping rather than abrupt on/off switching. | Martin et al., 2019, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2; Kim et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372. (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 4-4, martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 1-2, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 3-4, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 7-9) |
| Contour–hatch interaction | Slow, small-spot contours can penetrate deeply or keyhole; insufficient contour–hatch overlap leaves lack-of-fusion voids. Core vectors affected by galvo/timing error may stop before, or overshoot beyond, the intended interface. In a 1.27 mm wall, two contour/remelt zones occupy a substantial fraction of the width. | Adds interface-localized lack-of-fusion or keyhole pores and changes melt-pool geometry near both faces; nominally “core” porosity may therefore combine core, contour, and overlap behavior. | XCT experiments found near-edge contour porosity at a 0.05 mm hatch–contour offset, while the nominal 0.015 mm spacing did not show it; 0.03, 0.05, and 0.10 mm cases are compared in that paper’s Fig. 8. Other XCT work found small spherical/keyhole pores concentrated between perimeter and hatch. No primary study establishes a universal contour-free distance; a 0.2 mm face exclusion is plausible but unvalidated for the stated 50–70 µm contour spot and 130 µm core spot. (plessis2019effectsofprocess pages 3-7, englert2022concentricscanningstrategies pages 6-8, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 3-4) | Map pore density versus distance from each face rather than imposing only one cutoff; measure contour and core melt-pool boundaries separately; document contour order and offset; retain unchanged contours for screening but validate finalists without contours or in much wider cubes to isolate the core response. | du Plessis, 2019, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871; Englert et al., 2022, DOI: 10.3390/ma15031105; Kim et al., 2021, DOI: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372. (plessis2019effectsofprocess pages 3-7, englert2022concentricscanningstrategies pages 6-8, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 4-6) |
| Recoater / gas-flow orientation | Tall, slender walls can distort, swell, or protrude into the recoater path; a wall crossing the recoater presents repeated leading-edge interactions, whereas a parallel wall may guide the blade along its length. *Table: Key mechanisms that can make approximately 1.3 mm LPBF walls differ from bulk coupons, with quantitative precedents and practical controls. ---

### 1. Heat Accumulation in Thin Walls and Small Cross-Sections

Heat accumulation is the best-documented concern. In LPBF 316L stainless steel on an SLM 280 HL (single 400 W Yb fibre laser, Ar, 100 °C plate preheat, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, 275 W, 700 mm/s, VED ≈ 65 J/mm³), Mohr et al. measured a progressive rise in the pre-exposure (freshly recoated) surface temperature from ~100 °C at the base plate to ~545 °C at the top of a 114.5 mm cuboid when the inter-layer time (ILT) was only 18 s (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 3-4, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 6-8, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9). At 65 s ILT the top reached ~230 °C, and at 116 s it was ~170 °C (chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 9-10). These measurements were confirmed by a validated FEM model by Chaudry et al. (2022), which reproduced the layer-by-layer temperature rise to within ~7 °C for short ILT and ~30 °C for medium ILT (chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 7-9, chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 9-10).

The consequences for melt-pool depth and porosity are significant. Melt-pool depth in the upper section of the short-ILT cuboids was 13–19% larger than at intermediate or long ILT for the same VED (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9). At 275 W, 560 mm/s (high VED, ~82 J/mm³) and 18 s ILT, porosity in the upper section reached 1.1–2.7% (mostly spherical keyhole pores), compared with 0.1–0.2% in the lower section and ≤0.3% at longer ILT (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9). Sub-grain size also increased from 458 µm² (low VED) to 1386 µm² (high VED) for short ILT at the top of the build, while hardness dropped from 221 HV1 to 176 HV1 within the same specimen (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 6-8, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9). These ILT-dependent effects were also correlated with the ratio of area exploitation (RAE): the short ILT of 18 s corresponded to an RAE of only ~1%, representative of a single small part on a large platform (mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9).

For the user's build, each thin wall (~1.27 × 12.7 mm cross-section, ~7.6 mm tall) has a very short per-layer exposure time, but each comb part has seven walls plus a base, and twelve combs share the build. The effective ILT therefore depends on how many walls and how many parts are scanned before the recoater returns—a quantity that the Concept Laser M2 controller determines from the exposure order and can vary with parameter set. With 12 combs and ~84 walls, the layer time should be moderate, but higher-power / lower-speed walls that take longer to scan will experience a different ILT than fast, low-power walls on the same layer.

Piazza et al. (2020) independently demonstrated on miniature 316L parts (60–70 W, 25 µm layers) that melt-pool depth decreased linearly with build height in both cylindrical and conical geometries, attributed to heat accumulation raising the substrate temperature (piazza2020theeffectsof pages 3-7, piazza2020theeffectsof pages 7-9). They also confirmed that geometry affects the magnitude of the effect: the cross-sectional-area variation in a cone produced lower overall porosity than in a constant-section cylinder, because conical layers conduct heat differently (piazza2020theeffectsof pages 7-9, piazza2020theeffectsof pages 9-11).

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for 316L on SLM 280 HL; directly applicable in principle but quantitatively transferable to the Concept Laser M2 only with caution (different optics, chamber flow, build strategy). The referenced data are in Mohr et al. (2020, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080, Figs. 3, 7, 8, Table 1) and Chaudry et al. (2022, doi:10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x, Figs. 10, 12, 13).

---

### 2. Short Hatch Vectors, Scanner Turnaround, and Skywriting

In a ~1 mm-wide core (after contour exclusion), transverse hatch vectors are approximately 1 mm long. Each vector spends a large fraction of its duration in the acceleration and deceleration zones of the galvanometer mirrors. Martin et al. (2019) used in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging at 316L-relevant conditions to show that during turnaround, the vapor depression deepens as the galvanometer decelerates and the laser lingers near-stationary. The depression peaked approximately 100 µs after the reversal and approached steady state only after ~1000 µs. As the scanner accelerated away into a pre-heated region, the depression rapidly collapsed and trapped gas, creating spherical pores. In their experiments, **87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turnaround point** (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 1-2). At a programmed speed of 1000 mm/s, 89% of pores formed in under 500 µs (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 4-4).

**Skywriting** (turning the laser off at the end of each vector so that it does not expose the turnaround) does not reliably eliminate these pores: the abrupt transition from keyhole-mode exposure to zero power causes its own rapid depression collapse and can produce an end-of-track pore (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 6-6). The proposed mitigation is smooth, controlled power modulation that avoids keyhole formation and prevents rapid pressure changes in the melt pool (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 6-6).

Kim et al. (2021) systematically varied galvanometer acceleration and laser on/off delay on the NIST AMMT (IN625, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, 40 µm layers) and characterized the resulting pores by XCT. They identified two types of error: **following error** (galvo cannot physically follow the commanded acceleration, so actual track positions drift inward and do not reach the contour) and **synchronization error** (laser power switches too early or too late relative to galvo position). The galvo acceleration limit for the AMMT was ~10⁶ mm/s², and the calibrated position/power delay was 1.21 ms (plus ~0.05 ms for the laser to reach full power) (kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 6-7, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 7-9). With a 50× higher commanded acceleration, tracks oscillated within the core and never reached the contour, leaving an annular lack-of-fusion zone (kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 7-9). Revanur (2024) separately reports pipeline delays of 250–500 µs and point-exposure delays of 10–50 µs in LPBF galvo systems (revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 83-86).

For the user's build, a ~1 mm transverse vector at ~1350 mm/s requires only ~0.74 ms of steady travel—comparable to the total galvo response/delay budget. The fraction of each vector spent in acceleration/deceleration transients is therefore much larger than in a 12.7 mm longitudinal vector. This means transverse-vector layers will have more turnaround-related defects per unit volume than longitudinal-vector layers. The Concept Laser island scanning strategy (5 × 5 mm islands, vectors rotated 90° between adjacent islands, islands shifted between layers) further multiplies turnaround events (zeng2015optimizationofsupport pages 44-49). At 1.27 mm wall width, the core is narrower than a standard island, so the software must either assign a single stripe or treat the wall as a narrow feature. The exact behavior should be verified from the exported build file or CL WRX logs.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong (Martin et al. 2019, doi:10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2, in Nature Communications with 922 citations; Kim et al. 2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372). Machine-specific galvo and delay parameters are not transferable from the AMMT to the Concept Laser M2, but the physics is universal.

---

### 3. Contour–Hatch Interaction

In the user's build, contours at 100–120 W and 130–220 mm/s with a 50–70 µm spot produce P/v ≈ 0.45–0.92 J/mm—substantially higher linear energy density than the core hatch P/v = 0.274 J/mm at the production setting. The focused, slow contour is therefore more likely to operate in keyhole mode, and the contour–core interface is a known location for porosity.

Du Plessis (2019) studied 316L (EOS parameters, XCT) and found that increasing the hatch-to-contour offset from the nominal 0.015 mm to 0.05 mm introduced visible subsurface porosity near the part edges; at 0.10 mm offset the porosity was severe (plessis2019effectsofprocess pages 3-7). Englert et al. (2022) found, in their XCT analysis of hatching versus concentric strategies, that keyhole pores were concentrated specifically between the perimeter and the hatching region (englert2022concentricscanningstrategies pages 6-8). Kim et al. (2021) described near-surface pores close to the contour–core boundary, attributing them in part to laser control errors (following and synchronization errors) that truncate or extend tracks at the interface (kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 3-4, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 4-6).

In a 1.27 mm wall, contour regions on both faces may each penetrate ~0.1–0.2 mm inward (melt-pool half-width plus heat-affected zone), consuming 0.2–0.4 mm of the total width. After excluding 0.2 mm from each face, the remaining core window is only ~0.87 mm wide. This is narrow enough that contour-induced thermal effects (preheating, remelting, keyhole remnants) may still reach the center, especially at higher contour powers. No primary source was found that quantifies the exact contour-free depth for the stated parameters; the user should map pore density as a function of distance from each face to establish this empirically.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The mechanism is well supported, but quantitative width of the contour-affected zone has not been reported for the specific Concept Laser M2 parameters. Key references: du Plessis (2019, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871, Fig. 8) and Kim et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372).

---

### 4. Published High-Throughput Parameter Screening with Miniature Specimens

The closest published precedent is the NIST combinatorial LPBF approach by Weaver et al. (2021), who built a single specimen of IN625 containing 24 columns of 4 mm × 3 mm cross-section, each with a different combination of five laser powers and four scan speeds (60 unique conditions with post-processing variants). Porosity in the miniature combinatorial regions was below 0.03%, comparable to that of a larger 20 × 20 mm regular sample (weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 1-5). However, hardness was lower in the combinatorial regions, indicating a geometry or thermal-history effect, and **the authors explicitly cautioned that combinatorial-sample information is not equivalent to regular-sample information and that validation against bulk specimens is necessary** (weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 33-37). They recommended thicker porous dividers or unmelted-powder gaps between regions to reduce inter-column thermal coupling.

Fowler et al. (2024) at Sandia National Laboratories used 3 × 3 × 3 mm Kovar (Fe-29Ni-17Co) cubes in linear arrays on a Renishaw AM400 (50 µm layers), with 100–200 unique parameter sets per build plate, and characterized them by automated EBSD after surface grinding and dry electropolishing. They uncovered an **unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build** even for identical laser parameters (fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 1-2, fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 2-4, fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 4-5). This finding underscores that plate-position effects (thermal environment, gas flow, spatter) can be as important as the intentionally varied parameters and must be blocked or randomized.

Agrawal and Thoma (2022) demonstrated high-throughput surface characterization for 316L process screening, turning off contour and upskin parameters to isolate core behavior. The user's choice to keep contours fixed is a defensible alternative but adds the contour-interaction confound discussed above.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for the conclusion that miniature specimens can rank parameters, but moderate-to-weak for the claim that they reproduce absolute bulk density. Weaver et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109969, Figs. and Tables therein) is the most directly relevant reference.

---

### 5. Orientation Relative to Recoater and Gas Flow

The user's fourth panel is rotated 90° so that walls run across the recoater rather than along it, repeating 18 settings plus the control. This is a valuable blocking strategy. Several mechanisms can produce orientation-dependent results:

- **Recoater collision.** Tall, narrow walls that distort or swell above the powder plane can interfere with the recoater blade. Ti-6Al-4V thin walls showed substantial distortion even with supports, and unsupported walls could cause build failure (wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 8-10, wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 5-7). Walls perpendicular to the recoater present a leading edge on every stroke, while parallel walls may guide the blade along their length. The resulting powder-layer thickness variation can be asymmetric around the wall.

- **Gas-flow direction.** Spatter ejected from the melt pool is preferentially transported by the cross-flow. When scanning is opposite to the gas flow, larger particles decelerate and may redeposit on the same or adjacent walls; when aligned, spatter is more effectively carried away (cen2024modelingandsimulation pages 7-10, revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 18-22). Gas velocity decreases from inlet to outlet, creating a spatial gradient of spatter deposition and plume interaction (revanur2024novelscanstrategies pages 18-22). No primary study was found that quantitatively compares porosity in thin walls parallel versus perpendicular to the recoater or gas flow for 316L on a Concept Laser M2.

- **Plate-position and optical effects.** Laser incidence angle, focus offset, and spot ellipticity vary with distance from the optical axis. These can alter melt-pool depth and width systematically across the plate. The Fowler et al. (2024) observation of location-dependent microstructure at identical parameters is consistent with such effects (fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 2-4).

**Strength of evidence:** Mechanistic reasoning is strong, but quantitative orientation-specific data for the user's geometry and machine are absent. The user's paired-orientation design is itself a valuable contribution to the field. Key reference: Wu et al. (2020, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4).

---

### 6. Minimum Wall Thickness and Measurement Area for Porosity

No universally standardized minimum section area, pore count, or sampling protocol exists for LPBF metallographic porosity (sola2019microstructuralporosityin pages 11-12, sola2019microstructuralporosityin pages 16-18). Sola and Nouri (2019) emphasize that microscopic porosity measurements lack standardized imaging methods and are biased by magnification, focus, sampling location, and the number of images analyzed (sola2019microstructuralporosityin pages 11-12). Shahabi et al. (2022, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2022.112027) developed a statistical framework for determining data requirements for porosity characterization in LPBF; this paper was unobtainable for detailed review but is the key primary reference for this question.

In the user's design, after excluding 0.2 mm from each face and 1 mm from the top and bottom, the analysis window in each wall is approximately 0.87 mm × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm². This is comparable to but smaller than the 3 × 4 mm = 12 mm² regions used by Weaver et al. (2021), where porosity was <0.03% (weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 1-5). In the dense regime (<0.1%), a 4.9 mm² section at SEM resolution (sub-micrometer pixels) may contain only a few countable pores, making the area-fraction estimate highly uncertain. At higher porosity (>0.5%), the section may contain enough pores for a reasonable estimate.

Choi et al. (2024) addressed this by measuring all four longitudinal machined faces of Ti-6Al-4V fatigue bars, noting that multiple faces approach the bulk pore-size distribution better than a single section (choi2024opticalmicroscopyon pages 3-6). For the user's walls, measuring both halves of the bisected wall (mirror sections) would double the sampled area.

**Practical guidance:** The user's exclusion zones (0.2 mm from faces, 1 mm from base and top) are reasonable but should be justified empirically by plotting pore density versus distance from each boundary. The 0.2 mm face exclusion should be verified against the actual contour melt-pool boundary. All reported porosity values should include the analyzed area, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, number of pores detected, and a confidence interval (e.g., Clopper–Pearson or bootstrap). Convergence can be assessed by progressively enlarging the analysis window and observing stability.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The statistical framework exists (Shahabi et al. 2022) but was not fully reviewed. The qualitative guidance is well supported by multiple sources. Key additional reference: Sola and Nouri (2019, doi:10.1002/amp2.10021).

---

### Summary Assessment

Thin LPBF walls of ~1.3 mm thickness can serve as an efficient screening tool for ranking process parameters by porosity and melt-pool depth, as demonstrated by analogous miniature-specimen approaches (weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 1-5, weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 33-37, fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 2-4). However, they are **not** unconditionally representative of bulk material because:

1. **Heat accumulation** raises the temperature of thin, tall features and shifts the melt-pool regime toward deeper/wider pools and potentially into keyhole porosity—especially at high P/v and short ILT (chaudry2022experimentalandnumerical pages 7-9, mohr2020effectsofinter pages 8-9).
2. **Short scan vectors** in a ~1 mm core compress the steady-state fraction of each track and amplify turnaround-pore mechanisms (martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 4-4, martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 6-6, martin2019dynamicsofpore pages 1-2).
3. **Contour–core overlap** occupies a significant fraction of the 1.27 mm width, mixing contour and core porosity signatures (plessis2019effectsofprocess pages 3-7, englert2022concentricscanningstrategies pages 6-8, kim2021characterizingtheeffects pages 3-4).
4. **Orientation and position on the plate** introduce systematic biases from recoater interaction, gas-flow-dependent spatter, and optical-axis effects (wu2020exploringthefabrication pages 8-10, fowler2024highthroughputmicrostructuralcharacterization pages 2-4, cen2024modelingandsimulation pages 7-10).
5. **Small measurement area** limits the statistical precision of porosity estimates in the dense regime (sola2019microstructuralporosityin pages 11-12, weaver2021demonstrationofa pages 1-5).

The user's experimental design already incorporates several strong mitigations: scrambled Sobol sampling, repeated controls, two orientations, and SEM imaging. Additional recommended steps include (a) archiving the actual CL WRX scan files so that vector lengths, exposure order, and ILT can be reconstructed; (b) mapping pore density versus distance from each face to identify the contour-free zone; (c) comparing the production-set control walls with the production-set base blocks; and (d) validating finalist settings in wider (≥10 × 10 mm) density cubes before using the results to calibrate the Thermo-Calc AM Module or to seed Bayesian optimization.

*Table: Key mechanisms that can make approximately 1.3 mm LPBF walls differ from bulk coupons, with quantitative precedents and practical controls. Reported magnitudes retain their original material, machine, and processing conditions and should not be transferred directly to the Concept Laser M2.*

---

### 1. Heat Accumulation in Thin Walls and Small Cross-Sections

Heat accumulation is the best-documented concern. In LPBF 316L stainless steel on an SLM 280 HL (single 400 W Yb fibre laser, Ar, 100 °C plate preheat, 50 µm layer, 120 µm hatch, 275 W, 700 mm/s, VED ≈ 65 J/mm³), Mohr et al. measured a progressive rise in the pre-exposure (freshly recoated) surface temperature from ~100 °C at the base plate to ~545 °C at the top of a 114.5 mm cuboid when the inter-layer time (ILT) was only 18 s (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). At 65 s ILT the top reached ~230 °C, and at 116 s it was ~170 °C (pqac-00000032). These measurements were confirmed by a validated FEM model by Chaudry et al. (2022), which reproduced the layer-by-layer temperature rise to within ~7 °C for short ILT and ~30 °C for medium ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032).

The consequences for melt-pool depth and porosity are significant. Melt-pool depth in the upper section of the short-ILT cuboids was 13–19% larger than at intermediate or long ILT for the same VED (pqac-00000036). At 275 W, 560 mm/s (high VED, ~82 J/mm³) and 18 s ILT, porosity in the upper section reached 1.1–2.7% (mostly spherical keyhole pores), compared with 0.1–0.2% in the lower section and ≤0.3% at longer ILT (pqac-00000036). Sub-grain size also increased from 458 µm² (low VED) to 1386 µm² (high VED) for short ILT at the top of the build, while hardness dropped from 221 HV1 to 176 HV1 within the same specimen (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). These ILT-dependent effects were also correlated with the ratio of area exploitation (RAE): the short ILT of 18 s corresponded to an RAE of only ~1%, representative of a single small part on a large platform (pqac-00000036).

For the user's build, each thin wall (~1.27 × 12.7 mm cross-section, ~7.6 mm tall) has a very short per-layer exposure time, but each comb part has seven walls plus a base, and twelve combs share the build. The effective ILT therefore depends on how many walls and how many parts are scanned before the recoater returns—a quantity that the Concept Laser M2 controller determines from the exposure order and can vary with parameter set. With 12 combs and ~84 walls, the layer time should be moderate, but higher-power / lower-speed walls that take longer to scan will experience a different ILT than fast, low-power walls on the same layer.

Piazza et al. (2020) independently demonstrated on miniature 316L parts (60–70 W, 25 µm layers) that melt-pool depth decreased linearly with build height in both cylindrical and conical geometries, attributed to heat accumulation raising the substrate temperature (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029). They also confirmed that geometry affects the magnitude of the effect: the cross-sectional-area variation in a cone produced lower overall porosity than in a constant-section cylinder, because conical layers conduct heat differently (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for 316L on SLM 280 HL; directly applicable in principle but quantitatively transferable to the Concept Laser M2 only with caution (different optics, chamber flow, build strategy). The referenced data are in Mohr et al. (2020, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2020.101080, Figs. 3, 7, 8, Table 1) and Chaudry et al. (2022, doi:10.1007/s40964-022-00282-x, Figs. 10, 12, 13).

---

### 2. Short Hatch Vectors, Scanner Turnaround, and Skywriting

In a ~1 mm-wide core (after contour exclusion), transverse hatch vectors are approximately 1 mm long. Each vector spends a large fraction of its duration in the acceleration and deceleration zones of the galvanometer mirrors. Martin et al. (2019) used in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging at 316L-relevant conditions to show that during turnaround, the vapor depression deepens as the galvanometer decelerates and the laser lingers near-stationary. The depression peaked approximately 100 µs after the reversal and approached steady state only after ~1000 µs. As the scanner accelerated away into a pre-heated region, the depression rapidly collapsed and trapped gas, creating spherical pores. In their experiments, **87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turnaround point** (pqac-00000004). At a programmed speed of 1000 mm/s, 89% of pores formed in under 500 µs (pqac-00000002).

**Skywriting** (turning the laser off at the end of each vector so that it does not expose the turnaround) does not reliably eliminate these pores: the abrupt transition from keyhole-mode exposure to zero power causes its own rapid depression collapse and can produce an end-of-track pore (pqac-00000003). The proposed mitigation is smooth, controlled power modulation that avoids keyhole formation and prevents rapid pressure changes in the melt pool (pqac-00000003).

Kim et al. (2021) systematically varied galvanometer acceleration and laser on/off delay on the NIST AMMT (IN625, 285 W, 960 mm/s, 0.11 mm hatch, 40 µm layers) and characterized the resulting pores by XCT. They identified two types of error: **following error** (galvo cannot physically follow the commanded acceleration, so actual track positions drift inward and do not reach the contour) and **synchronization error** (laser power switches too early or too late relative to galvo position). The galvo acceleration limit for the AMMT was ~10⁶ mm/s², and the calibrated position/power delay was 1.21 ms (plus ~0.05 ms for the laser to reach full power) (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048). With a 50× higher commanded acceleration, tracks oscillated within the core and never reached the contour, leaving an annular lack-of-fusion zone (pqac-00000048). Revanur (2024) separately reports pipeline delays of 250–500 µs and point-exposure delays of 10–50 µs in LPBF galvo systems (pqac-00000007).

For the user's build, a ~1 mm transverse vector at ~1350 mm/s requires only ~0.74 ms of steady travel—comparable to the total galvo response/delay budget. The fraction of each vector spent in acceleration/deceleration transients is therefore much larger than in a 12.7 mm longitudinal vector. This means transverse-vector layers will have more turnaround-related defects per unit volume than longitudinal-vector layers. The Concept Laser island scanning strategy (5 × 5 mm islands, vectors rotated 90° between adjacent islands, islands shifted between layers) further multiplies turnaround events (pqac-00000041). At 1.27 mm wall width, the core is narrower than a standard island, so the software must either assign a single stripe or treat the wall as a narrow feature. The exact behavior should be verified from the exported build file or CL WRX logs.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong (Martin et al. 2019, doi:10.1038/s41467-019-10009-2, in Nature Communications with 922 citations; Kim et al. 2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372). Machine-specific galvo and delay parameters are not transferable from the AMMT to the Concept Laser M2, but the physics is universal.

---

### 3. Contour–Hatch Interaction

In the user's build, contours at 100–120 W and 130–220 mm/s with a 50–70 µm spot produce P/v ≈ 0.45–0.92 J/mm—substantially higher linear energy density than the core hatch P/v = 0.274 J/mm at the production setting. The focused, slow contour is therefore more likely to operate in keyhole mode, and the contour–core interface is a known location for porosity.

Du Plessis (2019) studied 316L (EOS parameters, XCT) and found that increasing the hatch-to-contour offset from the nominal 0.015 mm to 0.05 mm introduced visible subsurface porosity near the part edges; at 0.10 mm offset the porosity was severe (pqac-00000017). Englert et al. (2022) found, in their XCT analysis of hatching versus concentric strategies, that keyhole pores were concentrated specifically between the perimeter and the hatching region (pqac-00000018). Kim et al. (2021) described near-surface pores close to the contour–core boundary, attributing them in part to laser control errors (following and synchronization errors) that truncate or extend tracks at the interface (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

In a 1.27 mm wall, contour regions on both faces may each penetrate ~0.1–0.2 mm inward (melt-pool half-width plus heat-affected zone), consuming 0.2–0.4 mm of the total width. After excluding 0.2 mm from each face, the remaining core window is only ~0.87 mm wide. This is narrow enough that contour-induced thermal effects (preheating, remelting, keyhole remnants) may still reach the center, especially at higher contour powers. No primary source was found that quantifies the exact contour-free depth for the stated parameters; the user should map pore density as a function of distance from each face to establish this empirically.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The mechanism is well supported, but quantitative width of the contour-affected zone has not been reported for the specific Concept Laser M2 parameters. Key references: du Plessis (2019, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2019.100871, Fig. 8) and Kim et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.addma.2021.102372).

---

### 4. Published High-Throughput Parameter Screening with Miniature Specimens

The closest published precedent is the NIST combinatorial LPBF approach by Weaver et al. (2021), who built a single specimen of IN625 containing 24 columns of 4 mm × 3 mm cross-section, each with a different combination of five laser powers and four scan speeds (60 unique conditions with post-processing variants). Porosity in the miniature combinatorial regions was below 0.03%, comparable to that of a larger 20 × 20 mm regular sample (pqac-00000013). However, hardness was lower in the combinatorial regions, indicating a geometry or thermal-history effect, and **the authors explicitly cautioned that combinatorial-sample information is not equivalent to regular-sample information and that validation against bulk specimens is necessary** (pqac-00000014). They recommended thicker porous dividers or unmelted-powder gaps between regions to reduce inter-column thermal coupling.

Fowler et al. (2024) at Sandia National Laboratories used 3 × 3 × 3 mm Kovar (Fe-29Ni-17Co) cubes in linear arrays on a Renishaw AM400 (50 µm layers), with 100–200 unique parameter sets per build plate, and characterized them by automated EBSD after surface grinding and dry electropolishing. They uncovered an **unexpected, strong dependence of microstructure on location within the build** even for identical laser parameters (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). This finding underscores that plate-position effects (thermal environment, gas flow, spatter) can be as important as the intentionally varied parameters and must be blocked or randomized.

Agrawal and Thoma (2022) demonstrated high-throughput surface characterization for 316L process screening, turning off contour and upskin parameters to isolate core behavior. The user's choice to keep contours fixed is a defensible alternative but adds the contour-interaction confound discussed above.

**Strength of evidence:** Strong for the conclusion that miniature specimens can rank parameters, but moderate-to-weak for the claim that they reproduce absolute bulk density. Weaver et al. (2021, doi:10.1016/j.matdes.2021.109969, Figs. and Tables therein) is the most directly relevant reference.

---

### 5. Orientation Relative to Recoater and Gas Flow

The user's fourth panel is rotated 90° so that walls run across the recoater rather than along it, repeating 18 settings plus the control. This is a valuable blocking strategy. Several mechanisms can produce orientation-dependent results:

- **Recoater collision.** Tall, narrow walls that distort or swell above the powder plane can interfere with the recoater blade. Ti-6Al-4V thin walls showed substantial distortion even with supports, and unsupported walls could cause build failure (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). Walls perpendicular to the recoater present a leading edge on every stroke, while parallel walls may guide the blade along their length. The resulting powder-layer thickness variation can be asymmetric around the wall.

- **Gas-flow direction.** Spatter ejected from the melt pool is preferentially transported by the cross-flow. When scanning is opposite to the gas flow, larger particles decelerate and may redeposit on the same or adjacent walls; when aligned, spatter is more effectively carried away (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050). Gas velocity decreases from inlet to outlet, creating a spatial gradient of spatter deposition and plume interaction (pqac-00000050). No primary study was found that quantitatively compares porosity in thin walls parallel versus perpendicular to the recoater or gas flow for 316L on a Concept Laser M2.

- **Plate-position and optical effects.** Laser incidence angle, focus offset, and spot ellipticity vary with distance from the optical axis. These can alter melt-pool depth and width systematically across the plate. The Fowler et al. (2024) observation of location-dependent microstructure at identical parameters is consistent with such effects (pqac-00000043).

**Strength of evidence:** Mechanistic reasoning is strong, but quantitative orientation-specific data for the user's geometry and machine are absent. The user's paired-orientation design is itself a valuable contribution to the field. Key reference: Wu et al. (2020, doi:10.1007/s00170-020-05827-4).

---

### 6. Minimum Wall Thickness and Measurement Area for Porosity

No universally standardized minimum section area, pore count, or sampling protocol exists for LPBF metallographic porosity (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). Sola and Nouri (2019) emphasize that microscopic porosity measurements lack standardized imaging methods and are biased by magnification, focus, sampling location, and the number of images analyzed (pqac-00000039). Shahabi et al. (2022, doi:10.1016/j.matchar.2022.112027) developed a statistical framework for determining data requirements for porosity characterization in LPBF; this paper was unobtainable for detailed review but is the key primary reference for this question.

In the user's design, after excluding 0.2 mm from each face and 1 mm from the top and bottom, the analysis window in each wall is approximately 0.87 mm × 5.6 mm ≈ 4.9 mm². This is comparable to but smaller than the 3 × 4 mm = 12 mm² regions used by Weaver et al. (2021), where porosity was <0.03% (pqac-00000013). In the dense regime (<0.1%), a 4.9 mm² section at SEM resolution (sub-micrometer pixels) may contain only a few countable pores, making the area-fraction estimate highly uncertain. At higher porosity (>0.5%), the section may contain enough pores for a reasonable estimate.

Choi et al. (2024) addressed this by measuring all four longitudinal machined faces of Ti-6Al-4V fatigue bars, noting that multiple faces approach the bulk pore-size distribution better than a single section (pqac-00000037). For the user's walls, measuring both halves of the bisected wall (mirror sections) would double the sampled area.

**Practical guidance:** The user's exclusion zones (0.2 mm from faces, 1 mm from base and top) are reasonable but should be justified empirically by plotting pore density versus distance from each boundary. The 0.2 mm face exclusion should be verified against the actual contour melt-pool boundary. All reported porosity values should include the analyzed area, pixel size, minimum detectable pore size, number of pores detected, and a confidence interval (e.g., Clopper–Pearson or bootstrap). Convergence can be assessed by progressively enlarging the analysis window and observing stability.

**Strength of evidence:** Moderate. The statistical framework exists (Shahabi et al. 2022) but was not fully reviewed. The qualitative guidance is well supported by multiple sources. Key additional reference: Sola and Nouri (2019, doi:10.1002/amp2.10021).

---

### Summary Assessment

Thin LPBF walls of ~1.3 mm thickness can serve as an efficient screening tool for ranking process parameters by porosity and melt-pool depth, as demonstrated by analogous miniature-specimen approaches (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000043). However, they are **not** unconditionally representative of bulk material because:

1. **Heat accumulation** raises the temperature of thin, tall features and shifts the melt-pool regime toward deeper/wider pools and potentially into keyhole porosity—especially at high P/v and short ILT (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000036).
2. **Short scan vectors** in a ~1 mm core compress the steady-state fraction of each track and amplify turnaround-pore mechanisms (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).
3. **Contour–core overlap** occupies a significant fraction of the 1.27 mm width, mixing contour and core porosity signatures (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000045).
4. **Orientation and position on the plate** introduce systematic biases from recoater interaction, gas-flow-dependent spatter, and optical-axis effects (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000049).
5. **Small measurement area** limits the statistical precision of porosity estimates in the dense regime (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000013).

The user's experimental design already incorporates several strong mitigations: scrambled Sobol sampling, repeated controls, two orientations, and SEM imaging. Additional recommended steps include (a) archiving the actual CL WRX scan files so that vector lengths, exposure order, and ILT can be reconstructed; (b) mapping pore density versus distance from each face to identify the contour-free zone; (c) comparing the production-set control walls with the production-set base blocks; and (d) validating finalist settings in wider (≥10 × 10 mm) density cubes before using the results to calibrate the Thermo-Calc AM Module or to seed Bayesian optimization.

It does, however, show that scan-vector length and path geometry strongly alter the number of laser events and the locations of porosity. The hatching strategy has very short laser-on paths (3.19 mm average) and 70,310 laser-on lines, whereas the spiral strategy has 126.43 mm average paths and only 1,749 laser-on lines. Perimeter strategies are intermediate, with approximately 13 mm average paths. Shorter vectors therefore imply many more path ends, direction changes, and laser on/off transitions, creating more opportunities for transient energy-delivery errors at track ends or during scanner turnaround; the excerpt provides the trajectory statistics needed to motivate this interpretation but does not quantify those specific delay effects. Experimentally, the non-hatching strategies produced characteristic pores at acute-angle locations and 90° kinks, while large irregular pores also appeared where line spacing increased. The study further reports lack-of-fusion pores between tracks, especially where longer paths delay reheating of adjacent material. Thus, the excerpt supports a relationship between scan-path geometry, path-end/turnaround regions, thermal history, and porosity, but it does not explicitly attribute end-of-track pores to skywriting, galvanometer acceleration, or particular laser timing delays.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly supports the mechanism by which scan-vector turnaround can generate end-of-track or turnaround pores in LPBF. When the scan direction reverses in a serpentine pattern, particularly near part edges, the laser velocity decreases at the turnaround. If laser power remains effectively unchanged, the local energy density rises, increasing metal evaporation and producing a deep keyhole depression. Because this keyhole is unstable, it can collapse and trap shielding gas, creating a subsurface spherical pore. The passage also describes “edge-of-track” pores: voids between feedstock particles near the track margins can become engulfed by melt-pool flow and remain as small spherical pores. However, the excerpt does not explicitly discuss short scan vectors, skywriting, laser on/off delays, or galvanometer acceleration. Those effects are relevant because short vectors increase the proportion of time spent accelerating, decelerating, turning, and changing laser state; these transients can produce locally excessive or insufficient energy, potentially promoting keyholing or lack of fusion. Thus, the supplied text provides the clearest evidence for turnaround-induced excess energy and keyhole-pore formation, but not detailed evidence for the other scanner-control mechanisms.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that short scan vectors can increase porosity because the laser reaches turnaround points before a stable, steady-state melt-pool condition is maintained. During scanner turnaround, galvanometer mirrors decelerate before the turn and accelerate afterward; the instantaneous scan speed can approach zero, substantially increasing local energy density and dwell time. This produces localized overheating, deeper vapor depressions, and a transition from ordinary keyhole behavior into a deep-keyhole regime. The resulting vapor depression is associated with turnaround pore formation. The maximum depression occurs approximately 100 µs after the turn, attributed to heat buildup from the near-stationary laser, and then decreases toward a near-steady-state depth roughly 1000 µs after the turn. The excerpt also reports a strong time relationship between scan speed and pore formation: at a programmed speed of 1000 mm s−1, 89% of pores formed in under 500 µs, compared with 27% and 36% at 600 and 800 mm s−1. Thus, shorter vectors and rapid repeated turnarounds can disproportionately expose track ends to transient heating and deep keyholing. However, this passage does not specifically discuss skywriting or laser on/off delays; it primarily explains the contribution of scanner acceleration/deceleration and turnaround dwell to end-of-track or turnaround pores.

contexts.context: The excerpt attributes turnaround or end-of-track porosity to transient changes in laser energy density rather than simply to the existence of a short scan vector. During a scanner turnaround, galvanometer deceleration and reversal reduce scan speed while laser power may remain high, causing a sharp increase in local energy density and normalized enthalpy. The vapor depression therefore deepens into a keyhole. As the scanner accelerates away from the turn, especially into a pre-heated region, the depression rapidly collapses; rapid solidification then traps vapor and produces a pore. Short scan vectors increase the frequency and relative importance of these acceleration, deceleration, and turnaround transients, particularly in island scan patterns where there are many turn points per volume slice. Skywriting—turning the laser off at the endpoint—does not reliably prevent porosity: the abrupt transition from keyhole mode to zero laser input causes the vapor depression to collapse and can itself create an end-of-track pore. Finite laser on/off response delays further make the effective power change occur after the intended scanner position, aggravating endpoint defects. The cited mitigation is smooth, controlled power modulation that avoids keyhole formation, maintains the melt pool, and prevents a rapid power increase during acceleration out of the turn.
contexts.question: What is the effect of short scan vectors on porosity in LPBF? How do scanner turnaround, skywriting, laser on/off delays, and galvanometer acceleration cause end-of-track pores or turnaround pores in laser powder bed fusion?

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically discuss short scan vectors, scanner turnaround, skywriting, laser on/off delays, or galvanometer acceleration. It does, however, provide general context for understanding the porosity that can result from unfavorable scan behavior. Lack-of-fusion (LoF) porosity occurs when laser energy is insufficient to melt all powder in a layer, producing inadequate overlap between neighboring melt pools and leaving irregular voids between scan vectors. The text notes that porosity can be estimated from process parameters such as laser power, scan speed, layer height, hatch spacing, and melt-pool dimensions. It also explains that spatter can create or worsen LoF: unusually large spatter particles may remain on the powder bed, alter laser-material interaction, and cause insufficient melting beneath or around them. In addition, scan conditions that move melting away from conduction or stable-keyhole regimes promote spatter formation, which can subsequently contribute to LoF pores. Thus, the excerpt supports the broader point that local scan conditions and vector overlap influence porosity, but it does not provide the specific mechanism by which short vectors and scanner turnaround dynamics generate end-of-track or turnaround pores.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly quantify how short scan vectors create porosity or identify end-of-track pores by name. It does, however, describe the scan-control mechanisms that can produce nonuniform energy delivery at track ends and turnarounds. Short vectors require frequent scanner repositioning and direction changes. Galvanometer mirrors may need to stop and reverse, and rapid positional changes can cause vibration or “ringing”; insufficient settling time can therefore reduce positional accuracy. Laser modulation must also be synchronized with the delayed physical response of the optics. The excerpt reports a pipeline delay of 250–500 µs and point-exposure or drill-jump delays of 10–50 µs. If laser on/off timing does not compensate for these delays, the beginning or end of an exposure can be displaced relative to the intended scan path, potentially causing underexposure, excess exposure, or discontinuities that may promote pores. Skywriting extends the scan path while the laser is off so the mirrors can achieve a stable, approximately constant velocity before or after the active vector; without effective skywriting, acceleration and deceleration at short vectors can cause nonuniform melt-pool energy input. Thus, the source supports a mechanistic link between short vectors, turnaround dynamics, timing errors, and possible end-of-track porosity, but it does not provide direct pore measurements.
contexts.question: What is the effect of short scan vectors on porosity in LPBF? How do scanner turnaround, skywriting, laser on/off delays, and galvanometer acceleration cause end-of-track pores or turnaround pores in laser powder bed fusion?

At a scanner turnaround, the laser may continue delivering substantial power while the galvanometer slows, stops, and reverses. This transient overheating increases metal evaporation and produces a deep vapor or keyhole depression. When the depression rapidly collapses, liquid metal flows into the cavity and traps shielding gas, such as argon, in the solidifying melt, creating an end-of-track or turnaround pore. The excerpt does not explicitly discuss the detailed timing of skywriting or laser on/off delays, but these scanner-control transients can contribute to the same mechanism: if the laser remains on during nonuniform motion, excess energy promotes keyholing; if it switches off or on with a delay relative to galvanometer motion, the effective track endpoint and energy deposition are displaced, potentially leaving pores near the end of the vector. The study found that 87% of observed pores formed within 200 µm of the turn point. It proposes mitigating this effect by modulating laser power to compensate for melt-pool overheating and maintain approximately constant normalized enthalpy and vapor-depression depth.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that short scan vectors can increase porosity indirectly by causing melt tracks to cool and solidify before adjacent tracks or subsequent portions of the contour are deposited. At a turnaround or scan transition, the new vector may encounter a relatively cold neighboring track, producing inconsistent inter-hatch bonding and potentially lack-of-fusion defects. Small, shallow melt pools—which may result from insufficient energy or short exposure—also consolidate rapidly; in core regions this contributes to porosity and delamination risk, even though such pools reduce turbulence and spatter. The passage identifies skywriting or a short scan jump as the transition between vectors, but it does not separately quantify the effects of scanner turnaround, laser on/off delays, or galvanometer acceleration. Those mechanisms can plausibly worsen end-of-track or turnaround pores by reducing effective energy deposition near vector endpoints: acceleration and deceleration reduce the time spent at nominal scan speed, while laser firing and extinction delays shift the melt track relative to the commanded path. The resulting underexposed endpoint or overlap region may solidify before adequate remelting occurs, creating lack-of-fusion or end-of-track porosity. Thus, the excerpt supports a general link between short vectors, rapid cooling, and poor track bonding, but provides limited direct evidence about specific scanner timing and motion-control causes.

The model accounts for heat accumulation because, while layer n is scanned, the two previously deposited layers (n−1 and n−2) are also exposed to the heat source; thus, material layers receive heat more than once. contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative information about thermal history and geometry effects in LPBF 316L stainless steel, but it does not report the specific layer-by-layer temperature rise requested for thin-wall parts versus bulk material. It also gives no measured or simulated numerical temperature values, nor does it quantify the effects of inter-layer time or the number of simultaneously fabricated parts. The study compares cylindrical and conical geometries processed at 60–70 W and emphasizes that geometry changes heat extraction and therefore melt-pool dimensions. Heat transfer occurs through conduction to the substrate/build plate and convection to the shielding gas, while surrounding powder thermally insulates the part. Despite geometry-dependent heat extraction, the experiments found that melt-pool depth decreased in the building direction for all printed samples; this trend was not predicted by the analytical model. Thus, the excerpt may support discussion of geometry-dependent thermal behavior and heat accumulation mechanisms in general, but it does not establish that heat accumulation increases melt-pool depth with build height or provide the requested quantitative comparison between thin walls and bulk, inter-layer timing, or part count.
